dossier.whatItIs: The Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, Volume I, is a 63-page unclassified report published by AARO on 8 March 2024 under a congressional mandate to document the US Government's UAP record back to 1945. It covers the period from 1945 to 31 October 2023 and was largely prepared under director Sean Kirkpatrick before his retirement on 1 December 2023. A Volume II covering 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024 was promised and has not appeared.
dossier.whyImplicated: Volume I is the government's formal written denial that a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering programme exists, and as such it is the central artifact of the concealment argument rather than a rebuttal to it. It is an investigation of roughly thirty interviewees conducted without interviewing the most prominent complainant, written by the office whose own conduct several of the allegations concern, and published by the same office that decides which claims are in scope. Its own text concedes that an Intelligence Community Controlled Access Program had its scope expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering, which is the single most consequential sentence any US government UAP document has ever contained. It disposes of the rest of the record by attributing it to circular reporting among a group of people who worked on a real, congressionally funded Defense Intelligence Agency programme. Volume I is on this map because it is the document a concealment effort would have to produce, and because the promised second half has never arrived.
dossier.narrative:
The FY2023 NDAA, enacted December 2022, required AARO to produce a written report on the historical record of the United States Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena going back to 1 January 1945. AARO split the deliverable. Volume I would carry findings from 1945 to 31 October 2023. Volume II would carry anything derived from interviews and research completed between 1 November 2023 and 15 April 2024, on a date set by section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA. Volume I went to Congress in the first week of March 2024 and to the public on 8 March. Volume II has not been published.

The methodology is stated plainly in the report and is the first thing a hostile reader should notice. AARO reviewed official investigatory efforts since 1945, researched classified and unclassified archives, partnered with IC and DoD officials responsible for controlled and special access programme oversight, and conducted approximately 30 interviews. Thirty interviews is the entire human-source basis for a report covering seventy-eight years. AARO categorised the interviewees into tiers, with Tier 1 being those referred to AARO after speaking with Members of Congress or congressional staff. The report then states that none of the interviewees had firsthand knowledge of these programmes, that they were not approved for access and did not work on these efforts, and that this likely resulted in misinterpretation.

The findings are absolute in tone. AARO found no evidence that any USG investigation, academic-sponsored research, or official review panel has confirmed that any sighting of a UAP represented extraterrestrial technology. AARO found no empirical evidence for claims that the USG and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology. AARO has found no evidence of any authentic UAP-related NDA or other evidence threatening death or violence for disclosing UAP information. AARO has found no evidence that U.S. companies ever possessed off-world technology; the report says executives, scientists and chief technology officers of named companies met the Director of AARO and denied on the record ever having recovered, possessed or reverse-engineered such technology. A metal sample obtained from a private UAP investigating organisation and the US Army is assessed as a manufactured terrestrial alloy of magnesium, zinc and bismuth with trace elements including lead.

Against that, the report contains admissions its authors evidently regarded as harmless. It states that in 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering, that the programme never recovered or reverse-engineered anything, and that it was disestablished for lack of merit. It states that KONA BLUE was a Prospective Special Access Program proposed to the Department of Homeland Security, never approved, whose supporters never provided empirical evidence. It states that on 24 June 2009 Senator Harry Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III asking that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program and that Lynn declined on the recommendation of Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence James Clapper. It states that a named former CIA official signed a memo rejecting the claim that he had managed the movement of and experimentation on off-world technology, which means AARO went to that official and obtained a denial rather than a record. It states that an alleged 1961 Special National Intelligence Estimate circulating online is inauthentic.

The report's explanatory theory is that the modern allegations are, in large part, the result of circular reporting from a group of individuals who believe this to be the case despite the lack of any evidence, and that these individuals have been involved in various UAP-related endeavours since at least 2009, many of them connected to the cancelled DIA programme and the failed attempt to re-establish it under DHS as KONA BLUE. This is a genetic argument. It explains the allegations by the identity of the people making them rather than by testing what they allege, and it does so while conceding that the DIA programme was real, congressionally funded, and terminated over the objections of a sitting Senate Majority Leader.

The report also records lines of effort that are useful to this board regardless of its conclusions. AARO partnered with the archives of the Defense Intelligence Agency, the Central Intelligence Agency, the Department of Energy, the National Security Agency, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, the Services and the Combatant Commands, and with the US National Archives on locating UAP data. It interviewed five former Air Force members who served in and around intercontinental ballistic missile silos at Malmstrom, Ellsworth and other sites regarding a narrative of UAP over nuclear facilities. It records Captain Edward Ruppelt of Project GRUDGE noting concentrations of cases in the Los Alamos and Albuquerque area, Oak Ridge, White Sands, Strategic Air Command locations, ports and industrial sites.

One correction this board has already logged belongs here permanently. A full-text search of the released Volume I returns no occurrence of the term YANKEE BLUE. The widely repeated claim that AARO conceded that programme in Volume I does not survive a check of the document.

Volume I should be read as a primary record of what the United States Government said in March 2024, which is exactly the tier at which it belongs. It is not a primary record of the facts it asserts, and its authors have never produced the second half.

openQuestions: Volume II is overdue and unpublished. Its absence is the single largest gap in the government's own historical account and the first thing any oversight body should compel.

dossier.whatItIs: The All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office is the Pentagon body designated in July 2022 as the Department's authoritative office for unidentified anomalous phenomena. It was created under section 1683 of the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act, sits under the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, and absorbed the Navy's Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force. It publishes the statutory annual UAP report, runs a secure reporting mechanism for current and former government personnel, and produced the Historical Record Report.
dossier.whyImplicated: AARO is the single point through which every UAP record, contract and data holding in the Department of Defense was ordered to flow, which makes it either the instrument of disclosure or the instrument of consolidation, and the record supports the second reading. The office was given, by its own account, unrestricted statutory access to compartmented and special access material, then used that access to produce a report clearing the Department of every allegation made against it. Its own numbers show what the reporting channel actually does: of 262 people who came forward in a single year, 255 were declared out of scope and 7 were judged worth interviewing. Witnesses under oath before the House Oversight Committee have described being targeted after providing classified testimony, and one described a session he understood to be with AARO leadership as an effort to attack the credibility of UAP witnesses. AARO is on this map not as an arbiter but as a party: it holds the custody, it wrote the exoneration, and it decides who counts as a witness.
dossier.narrative:
AARO exists because Congress forced it into existence. Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA required the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, to stand up an office with a scope broader than the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group that the Deputy Secretary had created in November 2021. On 15 July 2022 Deputy Secretary Kathleen Hicks signed the memorandum that renamed and expanded AOIMSG into AARO. That memorandum is the founding document and it is worth reading for what it actually does. It makes AARO the authoritative office for UAP and UAP-related activities for the whole Department. It orders the Secretary of the Navy to disestablish the UAP Task Force and transfer its data, analysis and other relevant material. And it contains the sentence that matters most for this board: any DoD Component acting on behalf of the UAPTF, or who has data, analysis, contracts, or other material related to UAP, will immediately synchronize their efforts with the AARO.

That is a consolidation order. In a Department where the argument is that recovered material and its associated paperwork have been dispersed across contractors and unacknowledged compartments, an instruction that all UAP data, analysis and contracts route to a single office under USD(I&S) is the sort of instruction that can be read two ways. It is the necessary precondition for an honest accounting. It is also the necessary precondition for a controlled one.

AARO's first director was Sean Kirkpatrick, previously chief scientist at the Defense Intelligence Agency's Missile and Space Intelligence Center. He retired on 1 December 2023 having largely completed the Historical Record Report that his office published the following March. He publicly characterised David Grusch's allegations while, by his own later account, never having interviewed him. Grusch's position is that AARO never contacted him. Whichever account is correct, the resulting document is an investigation of a whistleblower's claims conducted without the whistleblower. Jon Kosloski, from the National Security Agency, took over in late 2024.

The office's own annual reporting is the best evidence about how the reporting channel functions. Under section 3373b of title 50, AARO hosts a secure mechanism for people claiming first-hand knowledge of a US Government UAP-related programme dating back to 1945. In the FY2025 report AARO discloses that between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025, 262 individuals used it. AARO determined 255 were out of scope. Seven warranted a request for a follow-on interview. That is a 97 percent rejection rate applied by the office whose own conduct is the subject of many of the allegations. The same report states, in language AARO chose, that the office is authorised by law to receive all UAP-related information at any level of classification regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs, and that generally no restrictions, including non-disclosure agreements, prevent AARO from receiving it. AARO therefore claims the access and simultaneously reports that almost nobody who comes to it has anything worth hearing.

The FY2025 report contains a second internal tension that a hostile reader should sit with. It states flatly that to date no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. Two sentences later it states that AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG, drawing on established procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel. An office that has found nothing is building a custody chain for the nothing it has found.

The performance record is poor by the Department's own inspector general's measure. DODIG-2023-109, whose unclassified summary was released on 24 January 2024, found the DoD had not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP, had issued no comprehensive UAP response plan, and had largely excluded the geographic combatant commands. The Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff each declined to provide official comments for the final report.

The delivery record is worse. Volume II of the Historical Record Report, covering interviews and research from 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024, was promised in Volume I under a deadline set in section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA. By late February 2026 it had not appeared, the FY2025 annual report had not appeared, the deputy director post was vacant, and Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough, asked why AARO had not published or briefed in over a year, told DefenseScoop the office had nothing to announce at this time. Gough did confirm that AARO had been examining over 2,000 UAP cases, roughly 1,000 of which lacked sufficient data and sat in an active archive. When the FY2025 report finally issued, it carried document number 26-P-0880 and a Department of War letterhead, with an information cut-off of 30 May 2025.

The strongest single item against AARO is in its own Volume I. The report concedes that in 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an Intelligence Community Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and that the programme was later disestablished for lack of merit. AARO's framing is that the compartment was unwarranted and empty. The fact remains that a compartment was stood up to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and the office that told us so is the office that closed it.

The same memorandum ordered that 'Any DoD Component acting on behalf of the UAPTF, or who has data, analysis, contracts, or other material related to UAP, will immediately synchronize their efforts with the AARO,' and directed the Secretary of the Navy to disestablish the UAP Task Force and transfer its data and material to AARO.

l0.label: YANKEE BLUE (alleged AFOSI indoctrination program)

dossier.whatItIs: YANKEE BLUE is an alleged United States Air Force practice in which personnel entering certain classified units were shown photographs of flying saucers and told they were being read on to a programme to reverse-engineer non-human craft, when no such programme existed. It was reported in June 2025 by The Wall Street Journal as a finding of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office under its first director, Sean Kirkpatrick, and was said to have been halted by a spring 2023 directive from the office of the Secretary of Defense. No primary document establishing the programme, the practice or the directive has been released.
dossier.whyImplicated: If documented, YANKEE BLUE would be the single strongest item in the concealment strand of this board, because it is the government manufacturing belief in a recovery and reverse-engineering programme inside its own ranks - which means that some fraction of insider testimony about that programme could be the product of a deliberate indoctrination rather than of access. It cuts both ways and it cuts hard, which is exactly why the tiering here has to be strict. What is documented is not the programme. What is documented is the Department's behaviour when asked for the paper: an Office of the Secretary of Defense FOIA search confined to a single correspondence office returning no records in September 2025, a Pentagon spokesperson on 1 October 2025 stating she could not confirm the memorandum with the word "alleged" underlined for emphasis, and an OSD appellate authority on 12 December 2025 overturning that search as inadequate and remanding for a new one. A department that cannot locate a Secretary-level directive from 2023 has either a records problem or a candour problem, and either is on the map.
dossier.narrative:
This entity is retained on the board with the allegation graded low and the negative findings graded high, and the distinction should be kept in front of the reader at all times. A negative primary finding is a documented fact. It is not a record of the thing.

The allegation entered the public record on 6 June 2025, when Joel Schectman and Aruna Viswanatha of The Wall Street Journal published "The Pentagon Disinformation That Fueled America's UFO Mythology." The reporting described a decades-long pattern in which the Air Force encouraged UFO belief to screen classified aviation programmes, and within that pattern a specific practice: personnel in certain classified units were briefed that they were being admitted to a programme called YANKEE BLUE concerned with reverse-engineering recovered non-human craft, shown photographs of saucers, bound by non-disclosure agreements, and in some accounts warned of extreme consequences for disclosure. The practice was said to have run from roughly the Cold War until 2023, when the office of the Secretary of Defense circulated a directive across the services ordering it to stop immediately. The finding was attributed to AARO's internal historical review under Sean Kirkpatrick.

Everything downstream of that article is either restatement or an attempt to find the paper. Popular Mechanics, VICE and the New York Post ran versions in June 2025; none produced independent documentation. The article itself, as researcher John Greenewald has noted, did not publish the memorandum, did not identify its date and did not describe its sourcing.

The documentary trail that does exist is a FOIA trail, and it is unusually clean because it has been published in full. On 17 June 2025 Greenewald's Black Vault filed a request with the Office of the Secretary of Defense for any directive issued in spring 2023 ordering a halt to YANKEE BLUE-related practices or to other activities involving fabricated claims of reverse-engineering non-human technology. OSD searched solely within its Correspondence Management Division and reported no responsive records. On 17 September 2025 an administrative appeal was filed arguing that a search confined to one office was not "reasonably calculated to uncover all relevant documents" under Oglesby v. U.S. Dep't of Army, 920 F.2d 57 (D.C. Cir. 1990), that a Secretary-level directive could reasonably reside in policy directorates or the OSD Executive Secretariat, and that agencies must pursue logical leads under Campbell v. DOJ, 164 F.3d 20 (D.C. Cir. 1998). The appeal also made the records-management point directly: any such 2023 memorandum would be subject to mandatory federal retention, so its absence is itself a finding.

On 1 October 2025, asked again about the WSJ claim, Pentagon spokesperson Susan Gough replied: "Regarding the alleged memo: I cannot confirm the existence of any department-level memo as described in the article. You may want to ask the Air Force or other military services whether they put out such a memo to their personnel." In the original email the word "alleged" was underlined. This is a carefully constructed sentence. It does not deny that the practice occurred. It denies confirmation of a department-level memorandum and redirects to the services. The Air Force did not respond to a request for comment.

On 12 December 2025 the Acting Chief of the OSD FOIA Division ruled on the appeal: "After carefully considering your appeal, and as a result of discussions between FOID personnel and this office, I am remanding your request to FOID for a search for responsive records." The appellate decision, released as case 25-A-3514-A1, does not establish that the memorandum exists. It establishes that the Department's own appellate authority found the Department's prior categorical no-records answer to rest on an inadequate search, and ordered it done again. As of the last published status the case remains open.

There is a second correction this board has already had to make about itself, and it belongs in the dossier. It has been widely repeated - including previously on this board - that AARO acknowledged YANKEE BLUE in its Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with UAP, Volume I, published 8 March 2024. It did not. A full-text check of the released 63-page volume returns no occurrence of the term, and it appears in none of the FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025 consolidated annual reports. The board logged that correction on 12 August 2026. The only official gesture toward the subject is the Department's statement, made in the context of the June 2025 reporting, that it "is committed to releasing a second volume of its Historical Record Report, to include AARO's findings on reports of potential pranks and inauthentic materials," then expected in late 2025. No such volume was located in the sources available for this dossier, which means the sole official channel through which the finding was to be documented had not delivered as of the research cutoff.

So the honest state of the record is this. A major newspaper reported a specific, named, dated practice sourced to a Pentagon office's internal review. The Pentagon has neither confirmed nor denied the practice, has said it cannot confirm the memorandum, has failed one FOIA search on appeal, has been ordered to search again, has promised a report volume that would address it, and has not published that volume. Every one of those is an artifact of an institution's conduct and every one of them is dated and attributable. None of them is the programme. YANKEE BLUE stays on this board as a node about the Department's disclosure behaviour, and it should not be cited by anyone as established fact about what was done to Air Force personnel until a document with a signature block exists.

l0.short: Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program

dossier.whatItIs: The Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program was a Defense Intelligence Agency effort solicited publicly on 18 August 2008 as HHM402-08-R-0211 by DIA's Virginia Contracting Activity and awarded on 22 September 2008 as firm-fixed-price contract HHM402-08-C-0072 to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, LLC of Las Vegas. Its stated objective was to understand the physics and engineering of breakthrough aerospace weapon system applications out to the year 2050 across twelve technical areas. It ran to 2012 and produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents plus a much larger body of work that has never been released.
dossier.whyImplicated: AAWSAP is the only documented instance in the modern record of the United States government funding a private company to study the physics of observed anomalous flight performance, and its own procurement file shows the seams through which such work escapes normal visibility. The solicitation was posted as a total small business set-aside under a classification code meaning 'Special studies and analysis - not R&D,' place of performance was the contractor's own facility, and the Top Secret facility clearance requirement was formally amended so that it was not required prior to contract implementation. The statement of work provides that any accountable property the contractor acquires with government funds becomes government-owned property and must be inventoried and returned within sixty days of contract end - a custody provision whose closeout has never been publicly documented. Senator Harry Reid asked the Deputy Secretary of Defense to convert the effort into a special access program on 24 June 2009 and was refused. The unreleased output of this contract, which its own government manager has described as running to more than a hundred detailed reports, is the largest identified block of missing documentary material in the modern record.
dossier.narrative:
AAWSAP is the best-documented UAP effort in the history of the United States government, and the reason is mundane: it was a competed commercial-items procurement, so it left a paper trail that the Freedom of Information Act could reach.

The solicitation went up on FedBizOpps as a combined synopsis/solicitation on 18 August 2008 under number HHM402-08-R-0211, issued by DIA's Virginia Contracting Activity at Bolling AFB, with responses due 5 September 2008. It was coded B, 'Special studies and analysis - not R&D,' under NAICS 541330, Engineering Services, and it was 'solicited as a total small business set aside' with a size standard of twenty-five million dollars. The Statement of Objectives, dated 18 July 2008, is unambiguous about what was wanted: 'The objective of this program is to understand the physics and engineering of these applications as they apply to the foreign threat out to the far term, i.e., from now through the year 2050. Primary focus is on breakthrough technologies and applications that create discontinuities in currently evolving technology trends. The focus is not on extrapolations of current aerospace technology.' Twelve technical areas were named, covering lift, propulsion, control, power generation, spatial and temporal translation, materials, configuration and structure, signature reduction, human interface, human effects, armament including directed energy, and other peripheral areas.

The qualification language is the tell. Offerors were asked to 'provide examples, conducted within the past 7 years, of having performed, as a prime contractor, the analysis, design, construction, and flight testing of high performance aircraft and/or satellites,' with the note that 'Success in this program is dependent upon this capability and experience.' The government was not shopping for a literature review.

The award document, Standard Form 1449, records contract HHM402-08-C-0072, awarded 22 September 2008 to BIGELOW AEROSPACE ADVANCED SPACE STUDIES, LLC, 4640 S Eastern Ave, Las Vegas NV, CAGE 54JU7, DUNS 827037768, with a total award amount of $21,948,810.00 and a base year of 22 September 2008 to 29 September 2009 followed by option years. The solicitation had anticipated 'a base year of 12 months from date of award plus four (4) 12 month option years' running to 30 September 2013. Deliverable line items were status reports, a project management plan for tasks 3.a.1 through 3.a.12, research reports for the same tasks, a Comprehensive Integrated Threat Assessment, travel and other direct costs.

Three provisions in the statement of work matter more than the money. First, security: 'The contractor shall comply with the terms and conditions of the DD-254 BEFORE initiating any classified effort,' and 'Contractor shall provide a work facility (including unclassified information systems) with a Top Secret Facility Clearance granted by the Defense Security Service (DSS).' But an amendment posted with the solicitation changed DD Form 254 Block 13 from 'THE CONTRACTOR WILL BE REQUIRED TO HAVE A TOP SECRET FACILITY CLEARANCE GRANTED BY THE DEFENSE SECURITY SERVICE (DSS) PRIOR CONTRACT IMPLEMENTATION' to 'THE CONTRACTOR WILL NOT BE REQUIRED TO HAVE A TOP SECRET FACILITY CLEARANCE ... PRIOR TO CONTRACT IMPLEMENTATION. HOWEVER, IT MUST BE OBTAINED AS SOON AS POSSIBLE DURING THE INITIAL YEAR OF THE CONTRACT.' The facility-clearance bar was lowered before award.

Second, place of performance: 'The work under this contract shall be performed at the Contractor's facility.' Third, and most consequential for this board, property: 'Any accountable property acquired by the contractor with government funds during the execution of this contract shall become government owned property. ... This property must be inventoried and returned to the government not more than 60 days after the end of the contract.' There is, in the released file, no closeout inventory.

What the contractor actually did is not seriously in dispute, and AARO concedes it. AARO's Historical Record Report states: 'Although investigating UFO/UAP was not specifically outlined in the contract's statement of work, the selected private sector organization conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA program manager. This research included: reviewing new cases and much older Project BLUE BOOK cases, operating debriefing and investigatory teams, and proposals to set up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials.' AARO adds that 'DIA did not seek, nor specifically authorize, this work though a DIA employee set up and managed the contract with the private sector organization,' and that the effort also investigated an alleged hotspot of UAP and paranormal activity at a Utah property then owned by the head of the contractor.

The special access question is the hinge. AARO records that 'On 24 June 2009, Senator Reid sent a letter to then Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program. Deputy Secretary Lynn declined to do so based on the recommendation of then-Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, James R. Clapper, Jr., that such a designation was not justified.' That refusal is documented in the FOIA record alongside DIA talking papers prepared for Reid's visits to the Director of DIA in January and May 2009 and an eighteen-page packet presented to the Deputy Secretary in November 2009.

AARO's account and the contractor's account of what the programme produced differ by an order of magnitude. AARO says the contract 'produced exploratory papers addressing the 12 scientific areas tasked in the contract's statement of work' which 'were never thoroughly peer reviewed,' and that it 'has yet to uncover any other substantive UAP case work.' The releasable record contains thirty-seven of thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. What is not in the record is the 494-page BAASS Ten Month Report, the Utah ranch investigation report, the personnel roster, obligation-by-year funding data, and the balance of the material that the government programme manager has described as running past a hundred reports. Under this board's sourcing rule, AARO's characterisation is a Tier 2 record of what AARO said, not a Tier 1 record of what exists.

dossier.whatItIs: The Defense Intelligence Reference Documents are a series of approximately thirty-eight unclassified technical survey papers commissioned from outside specialists under the AAWSAP contract and published by the Defense Intelligence Agency between roughly 2009 and 2011. They cover metamaterials, warp drive, traversable wormholes, antigravity, negative mass propulsion, quantum vacuum energy extraction, invisibility cloaking, high-frequency gravitational wave communications, and human biological effects of anomalous fields. Thirty-seven of the thirty-eight were released to The Black Vault by DIA on 25 March 2022 under FOIA case FOIA-0159-2018.
dossier.whyImplicated: The DIRDs are the most literal artefact on this board: a list, written by the United States government's own defence intelligence agency, of every theoretical route by which the observed flight performance of anomalous objects might be achieved. Read as a set, they are not a scattershot survey but a systematic decomposition of a capability - lift without visible propulsion, translation in space and time, signature reduction, materials that do not behave conventionally, and the effects such a craft would have on a human body standing near it. The government commissioned this taxonomy in 2008 and 2009 while the same contract was running field investigation teams and proposing laboratories to examine recovered material. One of the thirty-eight, the classified SECRET version of 'State of the Art and Evolution of High-Energy Laser Weapons,' has never been released and was not even acknowledged as withheld in the release letter, which is why the requester appealed on the adequacy of the search rather than on an exemption.
dossier.narrative:
There is a way of reading the DIRD series that makes it the single most informative document set on this board, and it is simply to read the titles in order and ask what question they collectively answer.

The released thirty-seven include 'Metallic Glasses - Status and Prospects for Aerospace Applications,' 'Aerospace Applications of Programmable Matter,' 'Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms,' 'Metamaterials for Aerospace Applications' and 'Metallic Spintronics' - the materials question. They include 'Positron Aerospace Propulsion,' 'Inertial Electrostatic Confinement Fusion,' 'Advanced Nuclear Propulsion For Manned Deep Space Missions,' 'Negative Mass Propulsion,' 'Aneutronic Fusion Propulsion,' 'Aneutronic Fusion Propulsion II,' 'MHD Air Breathing Propulsion and Power for Aerospace Applications' and 'Laser Lightcraft Nanosatellites' - the propulsion question. They include 'Warp Drive, Dark Energy, and the Manipulation of Extra Dimensions,' 'Advanced Space Propulsion Based on Vacuum (Spacetime Metric) Engineering,' 'Traversable Wormholes, Stargates, and Negative Energy,' 'The Role of Superconductors in Gravity Research,' 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications,' 'Concepts for Extracting Energy From the Quantum Vacuum' and 'Quantum Tomography of Negative Energy States in the Vacuum' - the physics-you-would-need question. They include 'Invisibility Cloaking - Theory and Experiments' and 'Detection and High Resolution Tracking of Vehicles at Hypersonic Velocities' - signature and detection. And they include 'Anomalous Acute and Subacute Field Effects on Human Biological Tissues,' 'Biosensors and BioMEMS,' 'Biomaterials,' 'Technological Approaches to Controlling External Devices,' 'Cognitive Limits on Simultaneous Control of Multiple Unmanned Spacecraft' and 'Cockpits in the Era of Breakthrough Flight' - the human question, which is to say, what happens to a person near one of these, and what would it be like to be inside one.

That is not a random reading list. It maps one to one onto the twelve technical areas in the AAWSAP statement of objectives: lift, propulsion, control, power generation, spatial and temporal translation, materials, configuration and structure, signature reduction, human interface, human effects, armament, and peripheral areas. The DIRDs are the deliverable structure of the contract made visible. And two of the titles are difficult to explain by any framing other than the one this board starts from. 'Anomalous Acute and Subacute Field Effects on Human Biological Tissues' is a medical paper about injury from proximity to something. 'Cockpits in the Era of Breakthrough Flight' is a human factors paper about operating a vehicle that does not exist.

The release history is its own artefact. Eric Davis, who worked for Bigelow Aerospace and BAASS, said on Coast to Coast AM on 28 January 2018 that thirty-eight such reports had been produced under AAWSAP. Within forty-eight hours The Black Vault filed for all of them; the request became FOIA case FOIA-0159-2018. In January 2019 a listing breakdown of the reports arrived under a separate case, FOIA-0033-2019, though a slightly different version of the list had already leaked. DIA completed the main request more than four years later, on 25 March 2022, releasing thirty-seven of the thirty-eight. The one that did not come out was the SECRET-classified version of 'State of the Art and Evolution of High-Energy Laser Weapons.' Critically, it was not listed as withheld. The release letter did not reference it at all, which is why the appeal was filed on the adequacy of DIA's search rather than on the applicability of an exemption - a procedurally different and, for a board about concealment, a more interesting posture. An unclassified version of that same paper, DIRD 23, is in the released set at thirty-one pages.

The DIRDs also function as a personnel map. The authorship of the series connects the private technical layer catalogued elsewhere on this board directly to a DIA contract: the space-time metric engineering and quantum vacuum papers, the wormhole and warp drive papers, and the materials papers were written by named specialists who reappear later at To The Stars Academy, at EarthTech International, and in the disclosure hearings of 2023 to 2025. The government did not go to a federal laboratory or an FFRDC for this survey. It went to a small network of physicists with an existing interest in the subject, through a small business set-aside contract, performed at the contractor's own facility.

What the series does not contain is equally important and should be stated plainly. No DIRD reports an examination of recovered material. No DIRD describes a craft. They are literature surveys and theoretical assessments, and several of them conclude that the routes they examine are not presently achievable. AARO's characterisation is that they were 'exploratory papers addressing the 12 scientific areas tasked in the contract's statement of work' which 'were never thoroughly peer reviewed.' On the face of the documents, that is accurate.

The argument for their place on this map is therefore not that they contain the secret. It is that they define its shape. A government office that believed it was looking at nothing would not commission a paper on the acute and subacute effects of anomalous fields on human biological tissue. A programme whose only interest was foreign aerospace threat out to 2050 would not need a survey of traversable wormholes. The DIRDs are the negative space around an object: thirty-eight independent attempts to explain, from first principles, how something that had already been observed could possibly work.

dossier.whatItIs: The Defense Intelligence Agency is the Department of Defense combat support agency responsible for foreign military intelligence. Between 2008 and 2012 it managed the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program, the congressionally earmarked effort that produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents on advanced propulsion, materials and related subjects, executed under contract by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies. AARO has confirmed that the material generated by that programme remains in DIA's archived holdings.
dossier.whyImplicated: DIA is the only agency the United States Government has formally admitted ran a modern programme that commissioned studies on how one would build and detect craft with capabilities no terrestrial system possesses, and it is the acknowledged custodian of that archive today. Its programme manager approved a contractor's UAP field investigations that were not in the statement of work, including proposals to stand up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials, which is a documented plan for a materials exploitation capability inside a defence intelligence contract. When the Senate Majority Leader asked in June 2009 that the programme be raised to Special Access Program status, the Department refused; when DIA cancelled it, its participants immediately proposed reconstituting it under Homeland Security as a compartment explicitly justified by claims that relevant material existed. AARO's own explanation for the entire modern disclosure movement traces it back to this DIA programme and its people. DIA is therefore the acknowledged root of the modern record, the custodian of its archive, and absent from the National Archives UAP collection.
dossier.narrative:
In 2008 DIA posted a solicitation and awarded a contract to Bigelow Aerospace for what became the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program. The money came from Senate-directed appropriations rather than a Departmental requirement, a point the DoD Inspector General records plainly when it notes that the Department did not officially look at UAP again after Blue Book until select members of Congress initiated and funded a programme under DIA's direction. The programme ran from 2008 through 2012 in its various forms and produced thirty-eight Defense Intelligence Reference Documents covering advanced propulsion, warp drive metrics, traversable wormholes, metamaterials, invisibility cloaking, high energy laser weapons, and biological effects of anomalous exposure. DIA transmitted the list of titles and principal authors to Congress in January 2018.

AARO's own account of AAWSAP, in Historical Record Report Volume I and in its standalone KONA BLUE paper, is more useful to this board than AARO seems to have realised. It confirms the programme was managed by DIA from 2009 to 2012 and funded through congressional earmarks with Bigelow Aerospace as prime contractor. It confirms the stated purpose was investigating next-generation aerospace technologies across twelve specific areas including advanced lift, propulsion, unconventional materials and controls, and signature reduction. It then states that although investigating UFO or UAP was not specifically outlined in the contract's statement of work, the selected private sector organisation conducted UFO research with the support of the DIA programme manager, and that this research included reviewing new cases and older Project BLUE BOOK cases, operating debriefing and investigatory teams, and proposals to set up laboratories to examine any recovered UFO materials.

That sentence is the whole argument in miniature. A defence intelligence agency programme, funded outside the normal requirements process, with a programme manager who authorised his contractor to run field investigation teams and to propose materials exploitation laboratories for recovered UFO material. AARO's framing is that DIA did not seek nor specifically authorise this work though a DIA employee set up and managed the contract, which is an attempt to place the agency at arm's length from its own programme manager. It does not work. A contract managed by an agency employee, funded by an agency line, delivering to an agency archive, is the agency's programme.

The escalation attempt is documented. On 24 June 2009 Senator Harry Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that AAWSAP/AATIP be made a DoD Special Access Program. Lynn declined on the recommendation of then Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence James Clapper, who advised that the designation was not justified. Read against the concealment thesis, a request for SAP status is a request for a compartment in which recovered material could lawfully be held without disclosure, and the refusal is the point at which the effort had to find another home.

It found one, briefly. AARO's KONA BLUE paper states that when DIA cancelled AAWSAP/AATIP, several individuals involved advocated that the Department of Homeland Security take the effort over and fund a new version under the code name KONA BLUE. In 2011 the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology established KONA BLUE as a Prospective Special Access Program based on claims that relevant information and material existed and required this level of protection. Six months later the Deputy Secretary of DHS disapproved it and directed immediate termination. AARO's insistence that no data or material was ever transferred to DHS is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that a Presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed Under Secretary stood up a prospective compartment on the strength of a representation that material existed.

The custody question is settled by AARO's own words. Its KONA BLUE paper states that information associated with the activities conducted under the auspices of AAWSAP/AATIP remains within DIA's archived holdings. Whatever the thirty-eight reference documents, the field investigation files, the debriefing records and the case reviews amount to, DIA has them. That makes DIA a custody node on this map regardless of what one concludes about the underlying phenomenon.

The people matter. James T. Lacatski, a career DIA propulsion and missile intelligence specialist, was the programme manager who brought the subject to Senator Reid and who converted the contractor's deliverables into Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. He co-authored Skinwalkers at the Pentagon with Colm Kelleher, the biochemist who ran the contractor's field science effort, and George Knapp, the investigative reporter who first obtained and published the DIRD title list. AARO's Volume I addresses that body of work by describing the contractor's Utah property investigations, its interest in shadow figures, creatures, remote viewing and human consciousness anomalies, and its plan to hire psychics. AARO presents this as evidence the programme lacked merit. It is equally evidence that a defence intelligence agency programme was pursuing lines of inquiry it would never have funded without something driving it.

One further fact belongs on the board. AARO states that it partnered with DIA's archives for the historical review. Yet as of the National Archives Record Group 615 page's review date of 22 May 2026, DIA does not appear among the agencies with a UAP records transmittal to the National Archives. The agency that holds the acknowledged archive of the acknowledged programme has not, on the public record, delivered it to the statutory collection.

dossier.whatItIs: The PURSUE releases are the five dated tranches of UAP material published by the Department of War at war.gov/UFO between 8 May 2026 and 7 August 2026. Each tranche is posted as a paired download - a document bundle served from www.war.gov/medialink/ufo/ and a video bundle served from a CloudFront distribution - alongside a searchable database of individual records. The files carry originator-prefixed identifiers such as DOW-UAP-D###, DOW-UAP-PR## and FBI-UAP-D###, the first time the United States Government has issued UAP material under a single public numbering scheme.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the physical evidence of what the government chose to hand over when a President ordered it to hand something over. The ledger is therefore diagnostic in both directions. It confirms the archive: material spanning 1944 to 2026, FBI holdings, NASA crew audio, INDOPACOM reporting, all of it previously unavailable and now released without clearance. It also confirms the shape of the withholding: at least a hundred of the roughly 160 files in the first tranche carry redactions, and every serious analyst who examined them - Mellon, Graves, Gallaudet, Rojas - reported the same absence of coordinates, sensor parameters, altitude, timing and chain of custody, which are the precise fields that would permit independent verification. No tranche carries a manifest, an exemption citation, a FOIA case number or a provenance statement. The releases are the strongest available proof that the holdings exist and the strongest available proof that the release process was designed to be unauditable.
dossier.narrative:
Five tranches, over three months, from a Department web page. Release 01 on 8 May 2026, Release 02 on 22 May, Release 03 on 12 June, Release 04 on 10 July, Release 05 on 7 August. The portal states the sequence plainly: 'The Department of War just released the fifth tranche of records under PURSUE. The first tranche was released on May 8, 2026.'

The delivery mechanism is worth describing exactly, because it is not a records system. Each release offers two ZIP archives. The documents come from war.gov itself: Release 01 documents at 1.2gb, Release 02 at 70.1mb, Release 03 at 826mb, Release 04 at 227mb, Release 05 at 130mb. The videos come from a commercial content delivery network at d34w7g4gy10iej.cloudfront.net: 1.3gb, 5.6gb, 4.6gb, 1.4gb and 513mb respectively. There is no manifest file, no checksum, no metadata schema, no index of what was withheld. The portal offers a filterable database by agency, release, incident date, incident location and type - which is more structure than any prior US UAP release has had, and still less than any archivist would call a finding aid. At the time this dossier was compiled the portal's 'LATEST RELEASE' link still pointed to Release 04 while the banner above it announced Release 05, which tells you something about how the page is maintained.

The file identifiers are the most analytically useful artefact in the whole programme. Filenames visible on the portal include DOW-UAP-PR46-Unresolved-UAP-Report-INDOPACOM-2024, DOW-UAP-D098_Film-Analysis-of-Unidentified-Objects_1953, FBI-UAP-D025_Digital-Rendering_Airborne-Triangle_2002, FBI-UAP-D027_Digital-Rendering_Dark-Translucent-Triangle_2023, FBI-UAP-D031_Digital-Rendering_Large-Triangle-with-Red-Lights_2023 and FBI-UAP-D038 through D042, a run of digital renderings of multiple red lights dated 2026. Two things follow. First, the numbering is originator-prefixed, which means the tranches were assembled by pulling from multiple agencies' holdings under a single tasking rather than compiled from one department's files - a single-department dump would not need agency prefixes. Second, the Bureau is a substantial contributor, and its contributions run to the present: FBI-UAP-D038 through D042 are dated 2026, the year of release.

The imagery convention is itself a disclosure decision. A large share of the FBI material is published as 'Digital Rendering' - artists' reconstructions of witness accounts rather than sensor products. DefenseScoop's illustration caption for the first tranche describes an 'Actual site photo with FBI rendered graphic depicting corroborating eye witness reports from September 2023 of an apparent ellipsoid bronze metallic object materializing out of a bright light in the sky, 130-195 feet in length, and disappearing instantaneously.' A rendering cannot be independently analysed. It can only be believed or not.

On volume and redaction, the contemporaneous count is DefenseScoop's: 'The initial PURSUE tranche contained a little more than 160 files, with at least 100 of those including redactions, according to researchers and experts who are currently studying them.' Roughly five files in eight were released with material removed, in a programme whose stated purpose was to stop hiding material, and with no exemption citation attached to any redaction.

The substantive verdict from the people best placed to give one was delivered within a week and was unanimous on the technical point. Alejandro Rojas, whose Enigma Labs team was cross-referencing the drop against a database of over 200,000 public sightings: 'Although there is a lot of information here, there is little context. Case summaries without coordinates, sensor parameters, or altitude data make independent analysis very difficult.' Tim Gallaudet, who thought some of the videos showed genuinely anomalous behaviour including right-angle turns and formation flying: 'the ambiguity of the video content in particular is concerning as no metadata was included. Therefore, it is impossible to conclude that any of the objects were truly anomalous.' Ryan Graves, on what a useful release looks like: 'The real value is in records that include clear provenance, sensor context, metadata, chain of custody, date and location, and enough operational context to allow serious independent analysis. Ambiguous imagery without that surrounding data is hard for pilots, researchers, or the public to evaluate responsibly.'

Several of the same people noted that much of the first tranche was not new. The Australian researcher Grant Lavac: 'For those of us in the UAP research community, the newness of the data in this first tranche is underwhelming. Much of it is a compilation of documents that have been in the public domain for decades.' His countervailing point is the one this board accepts: 'the story here isn't necessarily the content, but the process of official acknowledgment.'

And there is a provenance problem that the releases themselves create. Jordan Flowers of the Disclosure Foundation raised it in the first week: the US Government's own documented mid-century practice of manufacturing false UAP documents as cover for real weapons programmes means some of what is being published as authentic government UAP records may be disinformation artefacts. 'If some of what is now being released to the public as authentic government UAP records are in fact disinformation artifacts from that era, the public deserves to know. Transparency requires not just releasing files, but accounting for their provenance and integrity.' PURSUE publishes without provenance statements, which means it cannot distinguish a genuine 1953 film analysis from a 1953 cover story, and neither can anyone downstream.

What the ledger establishes is therefore narrower and harder than the headlines suggested. The archive exists and is large. The Department was able to produce material from at least six agencies within eleven weeks of a presidential post. The material released is the unresolved residue, stripped of the fields that would let anyone check it, with a third to two-thirds of it redacted and none of it assessed. That is not the record of a government that has nothing. It is the record of a government deciding, file by file, how much of what it has to show.

dossier.whatItIs: Project Blue Book was the United States Air Force's public-facing unidentified flying object investigation, headquartered at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and running from March 1952 until Secretary of the Air Force Robert C. Seamans, Jr. announced its termination on 17 December 1969. It succeeded Projects SIGN and GRUDGE and logged 12,618 sightings, of which 701 were closed as "Unidentified." Its textual records were retired to the USAF Archives and subsequently to the National Archives, where they are open as 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm, publication T-1206, within Record Group 341.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Air Force's own termination paperwork states in plain language that Blue Book was not the channel through which serious UAP reporting flowed. The 20 October 1969 staff document signed by Brig. Gen. C. H. Bolender records that "reports of unidentified flying objects which could affect national security are made in accordance with JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11, and are not part of the Blue Book system," and in the same paragraph that "there is still, however, no evidence that Project Blue Book reports have served any intelligence function." That is a signed admission of a two-channel architecture: a public channel with a press office and a phone number, and a separate operational reporting channel whose corpus has never been inventoried, indexed or transferred to any archive. The same document shows the Air Force weighing where to store the Blue Book files specifically to manage researcher access, with the Secretary of the Air Force Office of Information agreeing to "rigidly limit the right of access" and to "screen researcher's notes." Blue Book therefore sits on this board twice: as the mechanism that absorbed and normalised public interest for seventeen years, and as a custody object whose public copy was deliberately shaped before release.
dossier.narrative:
Project Blue Book is the most examined document set in the history of the subject and the least useful, and both facts follow from the same cause: it was never the file where the answer would be.

The Air Force ran three named UFO efforts in sequence. Project SIGN began in 1948, Project GRUDGE followed in 1949, and Blue Book was stood up in March 1952 under Air Force Regulation 80-17, which required base commanders to provide a UFO investigative capability and Air Force Systems Command to continue the project. The Bolender document of 20 October 1969 describes the resulting establishment with some precision: "Project Blue Book has two officers, one NCO and one civilian assigned on a full-time basis," plus Dr. J. Allen Hynek as a scientific consultant until 1 July 1969. Four people, one part-time academic, and a stated mission to determine whether UFOs threatened national security and whether they exhibited advanced technology. For seventeen years this was the entire visible federal apparatus.

The Bolender document is the load-bearing artifact. It was written as the staff package recommending termination, was released to researcher Robert Todd in January 1979, and reads as an internal cost-benefit memorandum rather than a scientific finding. Paragraph 4 contains the sentence that reorganises everything around it: after noting that the 1953 Robertson Panel had already concluded UFOs posed no direct physical threat, the document observes that "in spite of this finding, the Air Force continued to maintain a special reporting system," then states that national-security-relevant reports move under JANAP 146 or Air Force Manual 55-11 "and are not part of the Blue Book system." JANAP 146 is the joint communications instruction governing CIRVIS reporting of vital intelligence sightings; AFM 55-11 governs operational reporting. Neither corpus has ever been assembled, declassified or transferred as a body. Whatever came up those channels between 1952 and 1969 is not in T-1206 and never was.

The same document then explains, in operational terms, why Blue Book was kept alive after its own premise was disclaimed. Paragraph 8 recommends that if Blue Book is terminated the records "should be transferred to an appropriate archive and preserved for historical value and to prevent charges that the Air Force is concealing facts." The reason given for preservation is reputational management, stated openly. Paragraph 9 goes further. Because witnesses had been promised confidentiality, "access to these records and the publications must be carefully reviewed and controlled," and the Secretary of the Air Force Office of Information judged that "an Air Force controlled archive away from the Washington, D.C. area is the most appropriate storage facility," because ready availability in Washington "would result in an inordinate workload in clearing investigators, providing documentation, and reviewing and clearing manuscripts." Air University agreed to take the files on three conditions: that SAFOI answer all queries, that SAFOI "rigidly limit the right of access to recognized, legitimate researchers," and that SAFOI "screen researcher's notes to insure that 'confidentiality' is maintained." The Air Force decided, in writing, where to put the archive on the basis of how hard it would be for the public to reach.

The public announcement two months later, Department of Defense release No. 1077-69 of 17 December 1969, carries none of that. It quotes Seamans that continuation "cannot be justified either on the ground of national security or in the interest of science," cites the Condon report and the National Academy of Sciences review, and closes with the three conclusions that have been repeated ever since: no reported UFO ever indicated a threat to national security, no "unidentified" case represented technology beyond present-day scientific knowledge, and no "unidentified" case indicated extraterrestrial vehicles. Read against Bolender, the first conclusion is a statement about a filing system rather than about the sky, because the reports that could affect national security were routed elsewhere by regulation.

Custody is the second reason Blue Book is on this map. The National Archives holds approximately 2 cubic feet of project and administrative files, 37 cubic feet of case files arranged chronologically, and 3 cubic feet of records relating to the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, arranged by OSI district and overseas command. NARA states that the textual records are available "excluding names of people involved in the sightings." The public Blue Book is therefore a redacted copy of the Air Force's own Blue Book, and the confidentiality rationale from Bolender paragraph 9 is the reason. NARA also states flatly that it "has been unable to locate any documentation among the Project BLUE BOOK records that discuss the 1947 incident in Roswell, New Mexico." The General Accounting Office found the same when it reviewed Blue Book Special Report No. 14 at Archives II during its 1994-95 Roswell audit: the analysis of sightings from 1946 to 1953 "did not mention the crash or the recovery of an airborne object near Roswell in July 1947." The single most famous American recovery event does not appear in the official American UFO file. That is either evidence the event did not happen or evidence the file was not where such events were recorded, and Bolender tells you which architecture the Air Force actually built.

What the record does not show is equally specific. The Bolender document carries sixteen attachments listed on a separate page. Several are known and were released separately; several have never surfaced. There is no public inventory of JANAP 146 CIRVIS traffic. There is no public accounting of the OSI material beyond the three cubic feet NARA holds. And the January 1985 Wright-Patterson fact sheet that NARA reproduces contains the categorical sentence "There are not now nor ever have been, any extraterrestrial visitors or equipment on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base" - a dated, attributable, institutional denial about a specific installation, which is exactly the kind of statement this board catalogues rather than weighs.

dossier.whatItIs: The UAP Science Advisory Council is an outside scientific advisory body assembled in June 2026 at the request of the White House and in coordination with AARO, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the FBI and other agencies, and chaired by Harvard theoretical physicist Avi Loeb. It reports to a higher-level interagency UAP Governance Board that met for the first time in mid-June 2026. All data shared with the council is unclassified.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the first standing outside scientific advisory body the US government has convened on this subject, which makes the terms on which it was convened the most informative thing about it. Its chair has stated in writing that 'All the data shared with the council will be unclassified.' A body with no clearances and no access to classified holdings cannot examine recovered material, cannot audit a special access programme operating under a DCSA carve-out, cannot compel testimony, and cannot verify a negative. Its function, on the record as constituted, is to apply scientific method to the portion of the record that nobody disputes and that the executive branch has already chosen to release. Its membership was drawn almost entirely from the private technical and advocacy layer - the Sol Foundation and the Galileo Project - rather than from the federal laboratories, FFRDCs or prime contractors where the custody allegations point, and the published membership lists changed three times in seventeen days.
dossier.narrative:
The council is best understood as a boundary object: an institution created at the seam between a declassification programme and a scientific community, whose terms of reference tell you exactly where the executive branch has decided that seam sits.

The origin story is not disputed by anyone involved. The Skeptics Society announcement of 15 June 2026 says the council was 'formed at the request of the White House and in coordination with the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the FBI, and other agencies.' Avi Loeb's own account, published on Medium and dated by the platform to 13 June 2026, says: 'Over the past week, I was tasked by the above organizations to create a research team of young scientists who will serve on this council,' naming the White House, AARO, ODNI, the FBI and all Intelligence Community members. The Sol Foundation's account says ODNI, with the support of the FBI, announced it. DefenseScoop obtained confirmation from an ODNI official that ODNI, alongside the FBI and DoD, established the UAP Governance Board 'to provide guidance, recommendations and coordination at the interagency level, bringing together military, law enforcement, the intelligence community, and other civilian agencies,' and that the board 'met for the first time yesterday' as of Wednesday 17 June 2026, without identifying the participants.

The membership is where the record becomes genuinely strange, and the board should record the instability rather than smoothing it into a single roster. Loeb's first post named a core research team of five: Richard Cloete, Regina Sarmiento, Matthew Szydagis, Devesh Nandal and Omer Eldadi. The Skeptics Society, two days later, published an alphabetised list of eleven, adding Tim Gallaudet, Garry Nolan, Michael Shermer, Peter Skafish and Jennice Vilhauer, and identifying Loeb as chair. The Sol Foundation described a fourteen-member council and additionally named Jacob Haqq-Misra and Ross Howard. Loeb's list supplied to DefenseScoop on 17 June named twelve and introduced Carol Cleland and Ben Lamm while dropping Sarmiento. His second Medium post, dated by the platform to 29 June, listed fifteen and added Liberty Vittert Capito, Robin Hanson and Kevin Knuth while restoring none of the dropped names. Four published lists in seventeen days, none of them identical, none of them issued by the government that convened the body. There is no charter, no Federal Advisory Committee Act notice, and no agency-published membership roster in the record reviewed here.

The operative constraint is stated by the chair himself, twice, in plain language: 'All the data shared with the council will be unclassified.' The Sol Foundation repeats it. DefenseScoop reports that Loeb 'confirmed that all of the data shared with the newly installed team will be unclassified.' Loeb also told DefenseScoop that the meeting cadence has not been decided, and closed with a formulation that is worth quoting exactly because it is candid about the position: 'We will make the best lemonade out of the lemons we are given.'

Set that against what the council would need in order to test the central allegation on this board. The custody claims concern material held at contractor facilities under special access protection. Under 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3), the Director of DCSA can be relieved of industrial security oversight of exactly such a facility by a Deputy Secretary of Defense-approved carve-out. Under DoD Directive 5205.07, no contractor employee may hand SAP material to a member of Congress or their staff without the approval of the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. A council with no clearances is on the outside of both of those doors. It cannot look at a carve-out programme, cannot subpoena a contractor, cannot inspect material, and cannot verify that the archival material it is given is complete. Its chair says the council's purpose is to advise on how to resolve the nature of UAP and, in support of the Governance Board, to 'assist in the timely coordination of declassification of UAP-related information, in accordance with Executive Order 13526.' That is a real function. It is also, structurally, an advisory role over the release of material that the classification authorities have already decided to release.

The second structural observation is about where the people came from. Loeb chairs the Galileo Project at Harvard; Cloete and Sarmiento are described in the Skeptics Society announcement as Galileo Project researchers. Nolan and Skafish co-founded the Sol Foundation; Gallaudet is a Sol senior adviser; Haqq-Misra sits on Sol's advisory board; Ross Howard leads Sol's production and was named to lead the council's communications. Nobody named to the council in any published list is identified as coming from a federal weapons laboratory, an FFRDC, a University Affiliated Research Center, or a prime contractor's advanced development organisation. The council is staffed from the community that has been asking the questions, not from the institutions that would hold the answers.

None of that is a criticism of the individuals, several of whom have argued publicly for exactly the kind of instrumentation and data quality that would move this subject forward. It is a statement about the shape of the instrument. The government convened an outside body, gave it distinguished members and a reporting line to an interagency board, and drew the boundary of its access at the classification line - the same line on the far side of which every substantive allegation this board catalogues is alleged to sit.

dossier.whatItIs: PURSUE - the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters - is the Department of War's UAP file-release programme, published at war.gov/UFO and launched with a first tranche on 8 May 2026. It stands on a presidential direction issued by Donald Trump on Truth Social on 19 February 2026 rather than on a statute or a published executive order, and it is run by the Department of War with support from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence across an interagency group that includes the White House, the Department of Energy, AARO, NASA and the FBI.
dossier.whyImplicated: PURSUE is the first time the executive branch has conceded, in its own words on its own website, that UAP records were 'hidden behind classifications' and that there are 'tens of millions of records' to review. That concession is the argument. It was made not by AARO, the office Congress created to resolve UAP, but over AARO's head by the Secretary of War at the direction of the President, through a portal that is not aaro.mil and a process that is not FOIA, not mandatory declassification review, and not the National Archives collection Congress legislated in 2023. AARO's role was reduced to preparing other agencies' files for posting on someone else's website. And the programme's declared editorial posture - a War Department official told DefenseScoop 'We are not providing any comment or assessment on the files overall or on any specific file' - means the government has published imagery while withholding the analysis it certainly holds, which is the precise shape of a controlled release rather than a disclosure.
dossier.narrative:
On 19 February 2026 the President posted on Truth Social. The Department of War now reproduces the text on its own UAP portal as the programme's founding instrument: 'Based on the tremendous interest shown, I will be directing the Secretary of War, and other relevant Departments and Agencies, to begin the process of identifying and releasing Government files related to alien and extraterrestrial life, unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP), and unidentified flying objects (UFOs), and any and all other information connected to these highly complex, but extremely interesting and important, matters. GOD BLESS AMERICA!' There is no executive order number on the page. There is no statutory citation. The authority for the largest UAP declassification effort in American history, as presented by the Department itself, is a social media post.

The portal's Directive section states what the Department says it is doing: 'In response to President Donald J. Trump's directive for transparency on U.S. government information regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP), the Department of War (DOW), with support from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), is overseeing government wide efforts to expeditiously find, review, identify, declassify and publicly release unresolved UAP-related records and historical documents in the federal government's possession. This is an unprecedented, historic undertaking that requires coordination between dozens of agencies and the review of tens of millions of records, many existing only on paper, spanning many decades.' It commits to 'releasing new materials on a rolling basis as they are discovered and declassified, with tranches posted every few weeks.'

The scope limitation is stated in the next paragraph and is doing more work than it appears to: 'The materials archived here are unresolved cases, meaning the government is unable to make a definitive determination on the nature of the observed phenomena.' PURSUE publishes only what the government has failed to explain. It does not publish the resolved cases, the analytic products, or the compartmented holdings. 'DOW will continue to conduct separate reporting on resolved UAP cases, as mandated by statute.' The statutory channel and the presidential channel are explicitly separated, and the presidential channel gets the unexplained material.

The interagency composition, from the 8 May press release, is: 'The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the Department of Energy (DOE), the DOW's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and additional components of U.S. intelligence agencies.' The inclusion of the Department of Energy is the item on that list that should not be passed over: DOE is the custodian of the Restricted Data and transclassified foreign nuclear information regime that the Senate's own 2023 findings named as a mechanism by which UAP records escape mandatory declassification review.

The posture of the principals is uniform and quotable. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth: 'These files, hidden behind classifications, have long fueled justified speculation - and it's time the American people see it for themselves.' Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard described ODNI as 'actively coordinating the Intelligence Community's declassification efforts with the Department of War'. FBI Director Kash Patel: 'For the first time in history, the American people have unfettered access to declassified government files on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomenon.' NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman framed it as a whole-of-government effort. The 8 May release also contains a sentence that concedes the analytic gap up front: 'While all of the files have been reviewed for security purposes, many of the materials have not yet been analyzed for resolution of any anomalies.'

AARO's position in this architecture is the diagnostic fact. A War Department official told DefenseScoop: 'AARO is responsible for coordinating the declassification of identified DOW files. AARO also prepares DOW files and files provided by other agencies for posting on war.gov/ufo. AARO will continue to conduct its statutory mission of detecting, identifying, analyzing, and resolving UAP. Any encounters described in these releases that are resolved in the future will be posted on aaro.mil.' The statutory UAP office is a preparation function for a portal it does not own. DefenseScoop states the point flatly: batches are dropping on war.gov/ufo, 'not the existing aaro.mil website.' The war.gov portal's own 'Learn More' section reverses the flow, sending readers who want 'other historical UAP records' to aaro.mil.

And then the posture that defines the programme. Asked about the release, the War Department official said: 'We are not providing any comment or assessment on the files overall or on any specific file, so that the American people can make up their own minds regarding the files.' That sentence is presented as humility. Christopher Mellon, former deputy assistant secretary of defense for intelligence, identified what it actually is: 'For years the public was told there was little to see. The scale of what exists is itself a revelation. That said, data alone is not disclosure. Releasing raw files without context may confuse more than clarify.' Mellon's sharper formulation to DefenseScoop: 'The more substantive concern is not that the government is trying to overwhelm the public with low-quality data - it's that it is releasing evidence without releasing analysis.'

The technical complaint is the same complaint from every direction. Alejandro Rojas of Enigma Labs: 'Case summaries without coordinates, sensor parameters, or altitude data make independent analysis very difficult.' Retired Rear Adm. Tim Gallaudet: 'the ambiguity of the video content in particular is concerning as no metadata was included. Therefore, it is impossible to conclude that any of the objects were truly anomalous.' Ryan Graves: 'The real value is in records that include clear provenance, sensor context, metadata, chain of custody, date and location, and enough operational context to allow serious independent analysis.'

That is the shape of PURSUE. The Department of War admitted the archive exists, published the parts of it nobody can interpret, kept the analysis, kept the resolved cases, kept the compartments, and instructed the public to make up its own mind.
