dossier.whatItIs: The Department of Defense, renamed the Department of War by executive action in 2025, is the cabinet department that has run every official US government UAP investigation from Project SIGN in December 1947 to AARO today. It holds the special access programme architecture, the counterintelligence organisations that respond to incursions on military installations, and the security review office that clears what its personnel may say in public. It is the institution against which the legacy programme allegation is principally made.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Department has controlled every official UAP investigation for seventy-nine years and, by its own inspector general's finding, still had no coordinated approach and no comprehensive response plan eighteen months after Congress ordered it to build one. Its structure gives it the two things a concealed recovery programme requires: an unacknowledged special access programme system whose existence need not be disclosed, and counterintelligence organisations designated as the first responders to any anomalous incursion on any installation or range. Congress has twice legislated as though it believes unreported UAP compartments exist, first by giving AARO statutory access notwithstanding all access controls, then by forbidding the expenditure of funds on UAP-related special access activity not reported to the intelligence committees. A former DoD official who managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council testified under oath that the United States is in possession of UAP technologies and that the effort is hidden from elected representatives. The Department's own Historical Record Report concedes that a controlled access compartment was expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering.
dossier.narrative:
The Department's UAP history is documented by its own inspector general. The first official DoD UAP activity was PROJECT SIGN, established by the Air Force Chief of Staff in December 1947. From 1947 to 1949 Air Force personnel investigated 243 reported sightings. In 1952 the Air Force Director of Intelligence initiated PROJECT BLUE BOOK, which investigated more than 12,000 sightings before its termination in 1969. Then, in the inspector general's own words, the DoD did not officially look at UAP again until mid-2000, when select members of Congress initiated and funded a programme to study UAP under the direction of the Defense Intelligence Agency. That sentence is worth pausing on. The Department's own watchdog records that the resumption of UAP work was not a Departmental decision at all. It was a congressional earmark inserted over the Department's disinterest, and when the Senate Majority Leader asked for it to be made a Special Access Program in June 2009 the Deputy Secretary of Defense declined on the advice of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence.

That forty-year gap is the load-bearing claim of the official account and the weakest point in it. The Department asks the public to accept that between BLUE BOOK's closure in 1969 and AAWSAP's standup in 2008 it did nothing on the subject at all, in the same period in which it was operating an unacknowledged special access programme architecture whose whole purpose is that its contents cannot be inferred from budget documents or organisation charts.

Congress does not appear to accept it. Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA forced the creation of an office. Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA forced the creation of a reporting mechanism usable notwithstanding non-disclosure agreements and free from reprisal. Section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA forced the historical report. Section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA went further and prohibited the use of authorised funds for any special access or restricted access programme activity relating to UAP that has not been reported to the congressional committees by the Director of National Intelligence, and extended the restriction to contractor Independent Research and Development. Legislators do not write funding prohibitions against activities they believe do not exist.

The Deputy Secretary's July 2022 establishment memorandum is the Department's own consolidation instrument. It made AARO the authoritative office for all UAP and UAP-related activities, disestablished the Navy task force, and directed every DoD component holding UAP data, analysis, contracts or other material to synchronise immediately with AARO. If material and paperwork from a legacy programme existed anywhere in the Department, that memorandum is the order that would have moved it, and it moved it into an office reporting to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security.

The inspector general's evaluation, DODIG-2023-109, is the best independent measure of the Department's conduct. Its unclassified summary, released 24 January 2024, found that the DoD had not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP; that DoD components had largely excluded the geographic combatant commands, the organisations actually responsible for detecting and preventing threats against the United States; that components had developed varying informal processes; and that the Department had issued no comprehensive UAP response plan. The evaluation notes that the Military Services and counterintelligence organisations had sent some UAP incident reports to AARO but that the Department does not formally require them to do so. It also records that the Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff each declined to provide official comments for the final report. That is three of the Department's most senior officials refusing to go on the record with the inspector general on this subject.

The response architecture matters as much as the analytic one. AARO's FY2025 report states that the military Services' counterintelligence, law enforcement and security agencies are the cognizant authorities responsible for responding to UAP incidents and incursions on all installations and ranges, and that AARO aims to fully implement the Joint Staff's classified UAP GENADMIN from February 2025. The doctrine governing what the United States military does when an anomalous object comes down on its property is classified, and the organisations that would execute it are Army Counterintelligence, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. Those are the same organisations that, in the concealment argument, would administer the silence.

Luis Elizondo, who told the House Oversight Committee in November 2024 that in his last government position he managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council, testified in writing that UAP are real, that the United States is in possession of UAP technologies, and that the country is in the midst of a multi-decade secretive arms race funded by misallocated taxpayer dollars and hidden from elected representatives and oversight bodies. He testified that a small cadre within the government has created a culture of suppression and intimidation including unwarranted criminal investigations and harassment, and that the Pentagon's public affairs office employs a professional psychological operations officer as the single point of contact for UAP inquiries from citizens and the media.

The Department's posture since February 2026 has been transparency by executive channel. Secretary Hegseth committed to full compliance with a presidential disclosure directive, and a War Department official told DefenseScoop that AARO was working in close coordination with the White House to consolidate existing UAP records collections and facilitate the expeditious release of never-before-seen UAP information. The releases run through a departmental website rather than through the statutory National Archives collection, which puts the pace and the redactions back inside the Department.

dossier.whatItIs: The Department of Energy is the successor to the Atomic Energy Commission and the custodian of the United States nuclear weapons complex, including Los Alamos, Sandia, Lawrence Livermore and the Pantex assembly and disassembly plant, operated through the National Nuclear Security Administration. Under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 it holds a government-wide classification authority, Restricted Data, that exists entirely outside the executive order classification system and is not subject to automatic declassification.
dossier.whyImplicated: DOE holds the one classification authority in the United States government that a legacy programme could hide behind indefinitely, because Restricted Data is created by statute rather than by executive order, applies government-wide, and never automatically declassifies. Its facilities are also the physical centre of gravity of the phenomenon's own documented history: the green fireball wave of 1948 to 1951 concentrated over Los Alamos and Sandia, Project GRUDGE recorded case clusters in the Los Alamos and Albuquerque area and at Oak Ridge, and Congress now requires AARO to report annually on incidents at nuclear weapons production, transportation and storage facilities. In the most recent reporting year the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chairman sent AARO fifty incident reports, a 177.8 percent increase over the prior year, every one of which AARO records as not reported as UAP. A former DoD official named DOE under oath as one of the agencies with a role and no accountability. DOE has not appeared among the agencies transmitting records to the statutory National Archives collection.
dossier.narrative:
The reason DOE belongs on a map of concealment has nothing to do with what anyone alleges and everything to do with statute. Restricted Data is defined by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and covers all data concerning the design, manufacture or utilisation of atomic weapons, the production of special nuclear material, and the use of special nuclear material in the production of energy. It is classified under the Act, not under an executive order. Everything else in the national security classification system flows from a presidential order, currently the 13526 lineage, and is therefore subject to automatic declassification at twenty-five years unless exempted. Restricted Data is not. It requires affirmative review before declassification, it cannot be declassified by an agency that did not originate it, and the authority is government-wide. DOE's implementing regulation is 10 CFR Part 1045, most recently overhauled by a final rule published in the Federal Register on 21 December 2018.

The practical consequence is that if a UAP incident occurred over a weapons production facility, a storage igloo, a transport convoy or a laboratory working on weapons physics, the record of it could be created as Restricted Data from the moment of its generation and would then be permanently outside the reach of the executive order declassification machinery that every UAP disclosure statute has assumed. The FY2024 NDAA's records collection provisions operate on federal records generally. They do not amend the Atomic Energy Act.

The history is dense. From late November 1948 through early 1951 a wave of green luminous objects was reported over New Mexico, concentrated near Los Alamos and Sandia and over other sensitive installations. On 16 February 1949 a conference at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory brought together laboratory director Norris Bradbury, Edward Teller, Frederick Reines, representatives of the FBI, the Atomic Energy Commission and the military, and Lincoln LaPaz of the University of New Mexico Institute of Meteoritics, who had personally observed the objects. LaPaz, after interviewing more than a hundred witnesses, advised the military and the AEC that the fireballs were most likely either unconventional defensive devices being tested by the United States or Soviet reconnaissance devices. The Air Force ran Project Twinkle from 1949 to 1951 to instrument the phenomenon, never fully implemented it, and concluded the objects were probably natural.

AARO's own Volume I preserves the pattern independently. It records Captain Edward Ruppelt of Project GRUDGE noting concentrations of cases in the Los Alamos and Albuquerque area, Oak Ridge, White Sands, Strategic Air Command locations, ports and industrial sites. It records that AARO interviewed five former Air Force members who served in and around intercontinental ballistic missile silos at Malmstrom, Ellsworth and elsewhere in connection with a narrative that UAP sightings near nuclear facilities resulted in malfunctioning missiles and a destroyed test reentry vehicle. It records that AARO continues to investigate these cases because of their potential impact on the readiness of the US nuclear programme. And it lists DOE among the agency archives AARO partnered with.

Congress has legislated the nuclear connection into permanent statutory reporting. Section 3373(k) of title 50 requires AARO's annual report to include the number and description of incidents of UAP associated with military nuclear assets, and separately the results of consultation with the Administrator for Nuclear Security regarding incidents at facilities or assets associated with the production, transportation or storage of nuclear weapons or their components, and with the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding nuclear power stations and fuel storage sites. That is a standing legal obligation on the nuclear weapons enterprise to account, annually, for anomalous objects over its facilities.

The FY2025 report is the most recent execution of it and the number is striking. AARO received fifty reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the NRC Chairman regarding unmanned aerial system incidents near US nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, a 177.8 percent increase over the eighteen reported the previous year. Forty-seven of the fifty occurred between 1700 and 0500 local. Five persisted at least an hour, the longest about three hours. AARO then adds the sentence that carries all the weight: none of these incidents were reported as UAP. The nuclear complex is reporting a rising volume of unexplained aerial activity over the most sensitive sites in the country and categorising all of it, in advance, as drones.

The 2015 Pantex incident is the clearest recent case. A Department of Energy report describes security personnel at the nuclear weapons assembly and disassembly plant near Amarillo observing a diamond-shaped object in September 2015, hovering and moving in a northerly trajectory at roughly ten to fifteen miles per hour, described by witnesses as around four feet tall and two feet wide at the base and thinner at the top, with conflicting colour descriptions. The object was tracked by ground radar and photographed from a nearby radar tower, and the imagery was analysed by DOE's Sandia National Laboratories. The report was released in more complete form during the 2026 executive-branch disclosure tranches after earlier heavily redacted releases.

Luis Elizondo, testifying in November 2024, listed the Department of Energy among the White House, CIA, NASA and the Pentagon as agencies that play a role in the UAP issue while no one seems to be in charge, leading to unchecked power and corruption. As of the National Archives collection page's 22 May 2026 review, DOE had no transmittal listed in Record Group 615.

dossier.whatItIs: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection is a statutory records collection at the National Archives and Records Administration, created by sections 1841 to 1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act and codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note. NARA established it as Record Group 615. Every federal agency was required to review, identify and organise its UAP records for disclosure and transmission, and to transfer publicly releasable digital copies in advance of 30 September 2025.
dossier.whyImplicated: The collection is the concealment argument reduced to an inventory problem, and the inventory is nearly empty. Congress wrote a statutory definition that expressly reaches records concerning technologies of unknown origin and non-human intelligence, which is a legislature drafting for the existence of the thing rather than the possibility of it. It then stripped out the two provisions that would have given the statute teeth, the eminent domain power over privately held recovered material and the independent Review Board modelled on the JFK Act, leaving agencies to grade their own homework. What arrived is the measure of what compliance is worth: as of May 2026 the collection lists transmittals from seven organisations, and the Central Intelligence Agency, the Department of Energy, the Defense Intelligence Agency, NASA and the military departments are not among them. A parallel executive-branch release channel opened in 2026 that routes disclosures around the statutory collection entirely.
dossier.narrative:
The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act, sponsored by Senators Schumer and Rounds, passed the Senate in July 2023 as an amendment to the FY2024 NDAA. In its Senate form it would have created an independent Review Board with authority over agency withholding decisions, and it would have directed the federal government to exercise eminent domain over any recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private persons or entities. Neither survived conference. What was enacted in Public Law 118-31 on 22 December 2023 was the records collection framework alone.

What survived is still remarkable as legislative drafting. The statute directs NARA to build a collection consisting of copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence, or equivalent subjects by any other name, with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects. Congress wrote three categories into federal records law. Unidentified anomalous phenomena is the neutral one. Technologies of unknown origin and non-human intelligence are not neutral at all; they are the categories a legacy recovery programme would generate. The clause about equivalent subjects by any other name is anti-evasion drafting aimed at codeword renaming. The exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects is there to keep routine drone and balloon traffic out. Legislatures do not build statutory taxonomies for things they believe do not exist.

NARA implemented it. It established Record Group 615, issued guidance to agencies through memoranda AC 26.2024 and AC 04.2025, and set the mechanics: agencies identify all UAP records in any format, make digital copies, attach prescribed metadata, and transfer. NARA accepts only digital versions. Agencies were to complete identification and organisation by 20 October 2024 and to initiate transfer in advance of 30 September 2025. One provision deserves particular attention. Where a publicly releasable record includes redactions, the agency must simultaneously transfer redacted and unredacted copies to NARA. The National Archives therefore holds unredacted originals of redacted UAP records that it does not publish, which makes NARA itself a custody node with material it is sitting on.

The results are the story. As of the Record Group 615 page's stated review date of 22 May 2026, the collection lists transmittals from seven organisations: the Federal Aviation Administration, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Office of the Secretary of Defense, the National Security Agency, the Department of State and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. That list is as notable for its absences as its contents. The Central Intelligence Agency, whose own historian documented decades of UFO cover story management, is absent. The Department of Energy, which holds the nuclear complex and the Restricted Data authority, is absent. The Defense Intelligence Agency, which AARO has confirmed holds the AAWSAP archive, is absent. NASA is absent. The Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force are absent, which means the services that ran Project SIGN, Project GRUDGE, Project Blue Book and Project Moon Dust have not appeared in the collection created to hold that history. AARO itself, whose Volume I lists partnering with the National Archives on locating UAP data as one of its four lines of effort, appears only through OSD.

The statutory architecture explains why. The Act imposes an obligation on agencies to identify their own records and to decide what is publicly releasable. There is no Review Board, no independent adjudicator of withholding, and no penalty for a null return. Independent tracking of the transfer deadline found that most agencies approached with records requests either produced nothing or did not respond at all. A statute that asks the holders of a secret to declare it, and provides no mechanism when they do not, produces exactly the collection that exists.

The 2026 development compounds rather than fixes this. A presidential directive in February 2026 launched a multiagency effort to identify, review, declassify and publicly release UAP records, with a centralised repository opened in May 2026 on the Department of War's own website and material issued in periodic tranches. The releases have included previously unseen material, including a Department of Energy report on a 2015 incident over the Pantex nuclear weapons plant. But the channel is executive, discretionary, and controlled by the departments whose compliance with the statutory channel was the problem. Jordan Flowers of the Disclosure Foundation made the point directly in February 2026, noting that Congress had already passed laws establishing a public UAP records collection at the National Archives and that the existing statutory framework gave the administration a path it was not using, while warning that classification nuances could produce misleadingly partial or incomplete disclosures.

The collection is therefore best understood on this board as an instrument that works and a compliance record that does not. The statute is the strongest UAP disclosure law ever enacted and it names the categories precisely. Record Group 615 is real, it is growing, and NARA is holding unredacted copies the public cannot see. Seven agencies have delivered. The agencies at the centre of the argument have not.

claims.text: Sections 1841 to 1843 of the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, now codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note, require NARA to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection and require each federal agency to review, identify and organise each UAP record in its custody for disclosure and transmission to the National Archives.

In February 2026 a War Department official stated that AARO 'has made progress to make UAP information available and transfer those records to the National Archives in accordance with federal law,' while AARO's own historical and annual reports remained unpublished and overdue.

dossier.denialPosture: NARA has made no substantive claim about the phenomenon and issues no denials; it is a records custodian executing a statute. Its published position is procedural, that it receives records from agencies on a rolling basis and will add to Record Group 615 as they are transferred. The absence of denial is itself significant: NARA has never stated that any agency has certified it holds no UAP records, and it publishes no compliance register.
openQuestions: NARA publishes no register of which agencies have certified compliance, which have made null returns, and which have not responded at all. Without it, the seven listed transmittals cannot be distinguished from a near total failure of compliance.
The statutory transfer deadline of 30 September 2025 has passed. No enforcement action, referral or public accounting of non-compliance has been identified.
NARA holds unredacted copies of redacted UAP records under the simultaneous transfer requirement. The volume of that unpublished holding is not disclosed anywhere.

Whether records classified as Restricted Data under the Atomic Energy Act are treated as within or outside the transfer obligation has never been addressed by NARA guidance, which matters directly for DOE and the nuclear weapons complex.

The relationship between the statutory Record Group 615 collection and the 2026 executive-branch release channel is undefined. It is not established whether material released through the executive channel is also being accessioned into RG 615, or whether it substitutes for it.
The Senate-passed Review Board and eminent domain provisions have not been reintroduced and enacted. Whether any subsequent NDAA restores them is a live tracking item.

USS Nimitz Carrier Strike Group Encounters, 10-16 November 2004
l0.short: USS Nimitz Carrier Strike Group Encounters, 10-16 November 2004

dossier.whatItIs: On 14 November 2004, during pre-deployment workups off southern California, the USS Princeton (CG-59) vectored two F/A-18F Super Hornets from VFA-41 aboard USS Nimitz (CVN-68) onto a radar contact. Four aircrew, including squadron commanding officer Cdr. David Fravor, visually observed a white, wingless, roughly forty-foot object above a patch of disturbed water. A later sortie captured the infrared video now known as FLIR1, which the Department of Defense formally released as an authentic unclassified Navy video on 27 April 2020.
dossier.whyImplicated: Nimitz is the modern case that cannot be argued away on witness quality, because the observation was multi-platform: an Aegis SPY-1 radar track held over weeks, four aircrew in two aircraft, and an ATFLIR recording. What happened to that data afterwards is the point. Fravor testified under oath in July 2023 that "the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken," and that no one from the government contacted him about it until Jay Stratton did so in 2009 on behalf of a Defense Department programme he had never heard of. Enlisted personnel from the Princeton and the Nimitz have separately said that unidentified individuals arrived by helicopter within a day and collected Aegis and aircraft data recordings; that account is testimonial and undocumented. Either way, the United States possessed the highest-quality sensor capture of an unexplained object in its history and produced no investigation, no incident report and no data package - until a compartmented programme quietly reached out five years later. That gap between the sensor and the file is the same architecture Bolender described in 1969.
dossier.narrative:
The Nimitz encounter is the case that made the modern era possible, and the reason it belongs on a map of the legacy programme is not the object. It is the handling.

Fravor's sworn statement to the House Oversight Committee, filed for the hearing of 26 July 2023, is the cleanest primary account and it is worth reading for the operational detail rather than the spectacle. He was commanding officer of Strike Fighter Squadron 41 attached to Carrier Air Wing Eleven, roughly two weeks into an at-sea period, briefed to lead a two-versus-two air combat training exercise controlled by Princeton. On launch, "we were told that training was going to be suspended for real world tasking." His flight was vectored west of the combat air patrol point. Critically, he records what the controller told him about the preceding fortnight: the Princeton "had been observing these objects on their Aegis combat system for the previous 2 weeks. They had been descending from above 80,000ft and coming rapidly down to 20,000ft would stay for hours and then go straight back up." This is not a single sighting. It is a two-week radar campaign by a cruiser's air defence system that generated no public record and no known written report.

At the merge the aircrew saw disturbed white water, then a small white object with its longitudinal axis pointed north-south, moving abruptly above it, with "no Rotors, No Rotor wash, or any visible flight control surfaces like wings." Fravor descended in a clockwise turn; the object shifted its axis to align with his aircraft and began a climbing turn in the same direction. At roughly half a mile it "rapidly accelerated and disappeared right in front of our aircraft," and the disturbed water was gone with it. The flight turned back toward the CAP point sixty miles east and the controller reported that the object had reappeared there on the Princeton's SPY-1 radar, having covered that distance in "less than a minute."

Back aboard Nimitz they mentioned it to the crew preparing to launch. That crew took the roughly ninety-second infrared video that would be released by the government in 2017. Fravor adds a detail about a second recording that has never surfaced: "What is not seen is the Radar tape that showed the jamming of the APG-73 radar in the aircraft." An electronic attack on a fighter's fire control radar off the coast of California is, by any ordinary standard, a reportable event.

And then, on his account, nothing. "What is shocking is that the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken, and after a couple of days, it turned into a great story to tell friends. Not until 2009 did Jay Stratton contact me to investigate what we observed. Unbeknownst to all of us, Jay was part of the ATIP . . . program led by Lue Elizondo out of the DOD." That single paragraph is the whole argument in miniature. The Navy's normal machinery - safety reporting, intelligence debrief, mishap investigation - did not engage. Five years later a compartmented Defense Department effort did, without announcing itself, and the resulting document circulated for years as what Fravor calls "the Unofficial Official Report." Fravor also notes that Lt. Cdr. Alex Dietrich, the other pilot in the flight, had been invited to the Pentagon multiple times to discuss the event and view other UAP videos while he had heard from no one at all - which means the government knew where the aircrew were and chose which of them to talk to.

Against that, there is a competing testimonial strand that must be tiered honestly. Petty Officer Gary Voorhis, aviation technician Patrick "PJ" Hughes and Senior Chief Kevin Day have described, in interviews and documentaries from roughly 2019 onward, unidentified individuals arriving by helicopter within about a day and taking Aegis data recordings, combat engagement centre recorders, optical drives holding radio communications and E-2 Hawkeye data bricks, with Voorhis instructed to erase even blank tapes. No document has ever been produced for this and no official Navy statement has addressed it. It is also not in tension with Fravor as often assumed: Fravor speaks for his aircrew and his squadron's tapes, the enlisted witnesses speak about the cruiser and the carrier's data systems. Both can be true. Neither is documented.

What is documented is the government's slow, deliberate concession of the artifact. On 27 April 2020 the Department of Defense issued a formal statement authorising release of three unclassified Navy videos, "one taken in November 2004 and the other two in January 2015, which have been circulating in the public domain after unauthorized releases in 2007 and 2017." It confirmed that "the U.S. Navy previously acknowledged that these videos circulating in the public domain were indeed Navy videos," stated that release "does not reveal any sensitive capabilities or systems, and does not impinge on any subsequent investigations of military air space incursions by unidentified aerial phenomena," and closed with the line that matters: "The aerial phenomena observed in the videos remain characterized as 'unidentified.'" Two things are conceded in that paragraph. The video is real, and there are subsequent investigations of airspace incursions by unidentified phenomena that a release could in principle impinge upon.

Fravor's closing testimony frames the oversight question the way this board frames it. He is explicit that the issue "is not about full public disclosure that could undermine national security" but about checks and balances, and he makes the structural point directly: "even Unacknowledged Waived programs have some level of oversight by the appropriate committee members in the House and Senate and this work that is said to be occurring from Whistleblower testimonies should not be exempt." That is a retired commander with a Top Gun background telling Congress, under oath, that he believes there is an activity operating outside the waived-programme oversight floor. Nimitz is on this map because it is the point where the sensor data, the missing file and the oversight gap all converge in one afternoon off San Diego.

claims.text: In sworn written testimony to the House Oversight Committee for the 26 July 2023 hearing, Cdr. David Fravor (USN, ret.) states that on launch his flight was told "that training was going to be suspended for real world tasking."

Fravor's statement records that the USS Princeton "had been observing these objects on their Aegis combat system for the previous 2 weeks. They had been descending from above 80,000ft and coming rapidly down to 20,000ft would stay for hours and then go straight back up."

Fravor describes an object with "no Rotors, No Rotor wash, or any visible flight control surfaces like wings" that aligned its longitudinal axis with his aircraft, then "rapidly accelerated and disappeared right in front of our aircraft" at approximately half a mile.
Fravor states the object reappeared on the Princeton's SPY-1 radar at the flight's CAP point roughly 60 miles east, having covered that distance "in a very short period of time (less than a minute)."
Fravor states that a second recording exists and has never been shown: "What is not seen is the Radar tape that showed the jamming of the APG-73 radar in the aircraft."

Fravor states: "What is shocking is that the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken, and after a couple of days, it turned into a great story to tell friends."

Fravor states that the first government approach came in 2009 from Jay Stratton, who "was part of the ATIP . . . program led by Lue Elizondo out of the DOD," and that the resulting document circulated as what he calls "the Unofficial Official Report."

Fravor states that Lt. Cdr. Alex Dietrich, the other pilot in the flight, "had been invited to the Pentagon multiple times to discuss the event and view other videos of UAPs" while he himself had not been contacted after 2009.

Fravor's closing testimony asserts an oversight gap: "even Unacknowledged Waived programs have some level of oversight by the appropriate committee members in the House and Senate and this work that is said to be occurring from Whistleblower testimonies should not be exempt."

The Department of Defense stated on 27 April 2020 that it authorised release of three unclassified Navy videos, one taken in November 2004, and that "the aerial phenomena observed in the videos remain characterized as 'unidentified.'"

The same DoD statement records that "the U.S. Navy previously acknowledged that these videos circulating in the public domain were indeed Navy videos," that they had circulated "after unauthorized releases in 2007 and 2017," and that the released files were posted to the Naval Air Systems Command FOIA reading room.

The same statement concedes the existence of an ongoing investigative effort, saying release "does not impinge on any subsequent investigations of military air space incursions by unidentified aerial phenomena."

Fravor testified under oath alongside Ryan Graves and David Grusch before the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs on 26 July 2023 in the hearing "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency."

claims.text: Former crew members including Gary Voorhis, Patrick "PJ" Hughes and Kevin Day have stated in interviews since 2019 that unidentified individuals arrived by helicopter shortly after the encounter and collected Aegis data recordings, combat engagement centre recorders and E-2 aircraft data drives. No document supports this and no Navy statement addresses it; the compiled case file that reports these accounts states expressly that the point "remains anecdotal and is not confirmed by documentation."
The FLIR1 video was recorded on a later sortie the same day by a weapons systems officer, Lt. Cdr. Chad Underwood, using an ATFLIR pod; Underwood did not see the object visually.

dossier.denialPosture: There is effectively no denial to catalogue, and that is itself the finding. The Navy acknowledged the videos' authenticity in 2019 and the Department of Defense formally released them on 27 April 2020 while stating that the phenomena "remain characterized as 'unidentified.'" No component has denied the Princeton's Aegis tracks, denied the encounter, or produced a resolution. The only official position that has ever been asserted about Nimitz is that the imagery is real and the object is unexplained.
openQuestions: Do the USS Princeton's Aegis SPY-1 recordings and combat information centre logs for 10-16 November 2004 still exist, and under what disposition authority were they retained or destroyed?
Does the APG-73 radar tape Fravor describes, showing jamming of his aircraft's fire control radar, exist in any Navy holding?

Was any contemporaneous 2004 report of any kind generated - safety, intelligence, mishap or operational - and if not, under what authority was reporting waived for a two-week Aegis track and a fighter radar jamming event?
What is the provenance, classification history and custodian of the document Fravor calls the "Unofficial Official Report," prepared following Jay Stratton's 2009 contact?
Who directed the collection of data recordings from Princeton and Nimitz, if it occurred, and under what authority? No FOIA release has yet produced tasking, travel or custody documentation.
Why was Lt. Cdr. Dietrich brought to the Pentagon repeatedly while the flight lead was not contacted at all, and which office issued those invitations?

dossier.whatItIs: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023 was submitted by Senator Charles Schumer on 13 July 2023 as Senate Amendment 797 to S. 2226, the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, and printed in full in the Congressional Record at pages S2953-S2959. It travelled into the Senate-engrossed NDAA as a freestanding division of fifteen sections. Its enforcement machinery - an independent nine-member Records Review Board, a federal exercise of eminent domain over privately held recovered materials, and a $20,000,000 authorisation - was removed before enactment, leaving only an archiving and postponement regime at sections 1841-1843 of Public Law 118-31.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only text ever adopted by a chamber of the United States Congress that legislates on the express premise that recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence exist and are held in part by private entities. Its definitions are not rhetorical: 'controlling authority' is defined to include any commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of such material, and 'legacy program' is defined to reach commercial, academic and private-sector reverse-engineering endeavours predating enactment. Six senators including the Majority Leader and the Vice Chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee put their names to a finding that records exist which have been shielded from mandatory declassification review by Atomic Energy Act exemptions and an over-broad reading of transclassified foreign nuclear information. The bill then directs the Federal Government to seize that material by eminent domain and hand it to a board explicitly barred from containing anyone who has ever worked on a legacy program. The provisions that would have moved custody, compelled testimony and paid for the effort are precisely the provisions that did not survive conference - which is the single most informative fact on this node.
dossier.narrative:
On 13 July 2023 the Senate Majority Leader rose and submitted an amendment to the defence bill. The Congressional Record entry is flat and procedural - 'SA 797. Mr. SCHUMER (for himself, Mr. Rounds, Mr. Rubio, Mrs. Gillibrand, Mr. Young, and Mr. Heinrich) submitted an amendment intended to be proposed by him to the bill S. 2226 ... which was ordered to lie on the table' - and what follows across seven pages of the Record is the most consequential UAP text in American law.

The structure is deliberately modelled on the President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992: a records collection at the National Archives, a presumption of immediate disclosure, an independent review board with the power to override agency postponement, and a sunset. The differences are where the argument lives. The JFK Act dealt only with paper. This bill deals with objects.

The findings section states the premise. Congress finds that 'Legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified or subject to mandatory declassification review as set forth in Executive Order 13526 ... due in part to exemptions under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 ..., as well as an over-broad interpretation of "transclassified foreign nuclear information", which is also exempt from mandatory declassification, thereby preventing public disclosure under existing provisions of law.' That is a named legal mechanism of concealment, identified by the Senate, and it points at the Department of Energy and the Restricted Data regime rather than at the Department of Defense alone. The next finding says the Freedom of Information Act 'has proven inadequate.'

The definitions do the load-bearing work. 'Controlling authority' means 'any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence.' A commercial company cannot be in physical possession of a thing that does not exist. 'Legacy program' is defined to include 'commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence that pre-dates the date of the enactment of this Act.' 'Non-human intelligence' means 'any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware.'

The Review Board provisions establish 'as an independent agency a board to be known as the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board"', appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, nine citizens, without regard to political affiliation. Board staff must be citizens 'of integrity and impartiality who ha[ve] had no previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin or the examination of biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence.' A statute does not write a conflict-of-interest bar against a category of person that Congress believes to be empty.

Then the section that made the bill unpassable. 'The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.' Such material 'shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination at a location suitable to the controlling authority of said material.' The Board would then decide whether the material constitutes technologies of unknown origin 'beyond a reasonable doubt', whether it qualifies for postponement, and 'what changes, if any, to the current disposition of said material should the Federal Government make to facilitate full disclosure.' The Board would also 'have access to all testimony from unidentified anomalous phenomena witnesses, close observers and legacy program personnel and whistleblowers within the Federal Government's possession.'

The money section authorised $20,000,000 for fiscal year 2024 and, pending appropriation, permitted the President to use 'such sums as are available for discretionary use.'

What was enacted on 22 December 2023 in Public Law 118-31 is three sections - 1841, 1842 and 1843 - creating the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the National Archives, requiring agencies to review, identify, transmit and disclose UAP records, and setting out grounds for postponement. There is no Review Board. There is no eminent domain. There is no authorisation of appropriations. There is no witness-solicitation mandate. The surviving regime asks the original classification authorities that hold the records to identify their own records and to invoke their own postponement grounds, and gives no independent body the power to say no.

That is the argument. The Senate wrote a bill whose operative theory was that the material is held by controlling authorities including private companies, that those companies will not surrender it voluntarily, and that only compulsory acquisition plus an outside board with special access clearances could break the hold. Conference removed compulsion and removed the outside board. What remains is a filing cabinet with the same locks and the same keyholders.

claims.text: S.Amdt. 797 was submitted on 13 July 2023 by Sen. Schumer 'for himself, Mr. Rounds, Mr. Rubio, Mrs. Gillibrand, Mr. Young, and Mr. Heinrich' to S. 2226, and was ordered to lie on the table; the full text is printed at Congressional Record, Vol. 169, No. 120, pages S2953-S2959.

Congressional finding (a)(4): 'Legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified or subject to mandatory declassification review as set forth in Executive Order 13526 ... due in part to exemptions under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2011 et seq.), as well as an over-broad interpretation of "transclassified foreign nuclear information", which is also exempt from mandatory declassification, thereby preventing public disclosure under existing provisions of law.'

The definitions section defines 'controlling authority' as 'any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence.'

'Legacy program' is defined to include 'commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence that pre-dates the date of the enactment of this Act.'

'Non-human intelligence' is defined as 'any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware.'

The Review Board section states: '(a) ESTABLISHMENT.-There is established as an independent agency a board to be known as the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board"' and '(1) IN GENERAL.-The President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, shall appoint, without regard to political affiliation, 9 citizens of the United States to serve as members of the Review Board.'

The Review Board staffing section requires that a person appointed to the staff 'shall be a citizen of integrity and impartiality who has had no previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin or the examination of biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence', and requires accelerated grant of 'all necessary special access program clearances'.

The eminent domain provision reads in full: '(a) EXERCISE OF EMINENT DOMAIN.-The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.'

The same section provides that '(b) AVAILABILITY TO REVIEW BOARD.-Any and all such material, should it exist, shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination at a location suitable to the controlling authority of said material', and that the Board shall decide 'whether the material examined constitutes technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence beyond a reasonable doubt'.

The Board was to 'have access to all testimony from unidentified anomalous phenomena witnesses, close observers and legacy program personnel and whistleblowers within the Federal Government's possession as of and after the date of the enactment of this Act'. The phrase 'legacy program personnel' is statutory text.

The authorisation section provides '$20,000,000 for fiscal year 2024' and adds that 'Until such time as funds are appropriated pursuant to subsection (a), the President may use such sums as are available for discretionary use to carry out this title.'

The National Archives states that it 'has established an "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection," per sections 1841-1843 of the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act (Public Law 118-31)', and that records received from federal agencies under that Act are accessioned into Record Group 615.

The disclosure machinery enacted in Public Law 118-31 consists only of the NARA records collection at sections 1841-1843; the Review Board, the eminent domain provision, the Review Board witness-access provision and the $20,000,000 authorisation have no enacted counterpart.

dossier.whatItIs: A hearing of the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability's Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, held 26 July 2023 at 10:06 a.m. in room 2154 of the Rayburn House Office Building, chaired by Rep. Glenn Grothman. The witnesses were Ryan Graves, David Grusch and retired Commander David Fravor. It was the first congressional hearing at which a former intelligence officer testified under oath that the United States operates a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programme outside congressional oversight.
dossier.whyImplicated: This hearing converted the legacy programme allegation from journalism into sworn testimony before a committee of jurisdiction, and it did so with three specific mechanisms attached: how the programme is hidden (special access programs the witness was denied read-on to), how it is paid for (misappropriation of funds and self-funding), and who holds the material (contractors, described by the witness as 'the metal benders', who are under no requirement to report UAP). Fravor's written statement establishes that the most corroborated modern military encounter was never investigated and the tapes were never collected - an evidentiary vacuum that is itself the artefact. The hearing also demonstrated the ceiling on congressional capability: members were denied a SCIF, no contractor was called, no document production was compelled, and every substantive answer was deferred to a closed session that has never been publicly confirmed to have occurred on these terms. The committee's own wrap-up release then framed the day around pilot reporting and stigma, omitting the crash retrieval testimony entirely.
dossier.narrative:
The subcommittee met at 10:06 a.m. on 26 July 2023 in 2154 Rayburn. Present were Representatives Grothman, Gosar, Foxx, Sessions, Biggs, Mace, LaTurner, Armstrong, Perry, Garcia, Moskowitz and Frost; also present, waived on, were Luna, Burlison, Gaetz, Burchett, Comer, Ogles, Langworthy, Raskin and Ocasio-Cortez. The unusual size of the 'also present' list is the first fact about this hearing: members from outside the subcommittee, from both parties, came to sit in.

The second fact came in Burchett's opening. Members, he said, 'were even denied access to a classified briefing in a SCIF prior to this hearing due to the amount of hoops that we had to jump through to grant temporary clearance to witness Grusch, who has knowledge of classified information.' The committee therefore held a public hearing about compartmented programmes without the means to hear about compartmented programmes. Every subsequent deferral in the transcript traces back to that.

Grusch's written opening statement is the core document. He identifies himself as an intelligence officer of fourteen years, a USAF major, and from 2021 to 2023 a GS-15 at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, where he was his agency's co-lead for UAP and transmedium object analysis reporting to the UAP Task Force and then to AARO. He states that he became a whistleblower 'through a PPD-19 Urgent Concern filing with the Intelligence Community Inspector General (ICIG)'. He describes a specific tasking: 'In 2019, the UAPTF director tasked me to identify all Special Access Programs & Controlled Access Programs (SAPs/CAPs) we needed to satisfy our congressionally mandated mission.' And then the sentence the hearing is remembered for: 'I was informed, in the course of my official duties, of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program to which I was denied access to those additional read-on's.' His closing statement calls the programmes he reported the 'Non-Human Reverse Engineering Programs' and predicts their revelation would act as 'an ontological (earth-shattering) shock'.

Under questioning the mechanism claims sharpened. Asked by Rep. Moskowitz how such a programme gets funded, Grusch answered: 'I will give you generalities. I can get very specific in a closed session. But misappropriation of funds and self-fund.' Asked whether that meant money budgeted for one programme goes elsewhere, he said 'Yes. I have specific knowledge of that. Yes.' Asked by Rep. Ocasio-Cortez about interactions between defence contractors and UAP activities, he described 'the contractors, you know, or the metal benders, so to speak, the ones actually doing specific performance on government contracts.' Asked whether those contractors are required to report UAP sightings, he answered: 'In terms of the contractors? Not that I am aware of.' That single exchange is the cleanest statement on the record of the regulatory gap that would allow contractor custody to persist without disclosure.

On where and who, he refused in open session and said the information had gone elsewhere: 'I cannot discuss that publicly, but I did provide that information both to the intel committees and the Inspector General.' Asked by Burchett whether it could be given in a SCIF, he replied 'Sure, if you had the appropriate accesses.' Asked when the government first became aware, he said: 'I like to use the term nonhuman. I do not like to denote origin. Keeps the aperture open both scientifically. Certainly, like I have discussed publicly, previously 1930's.' Asked by Rep. Burlison whether he had personally seen the craft or bodies, he distinguished carefully: on the craft, 'I have to be careful to describe what I have seen firsthand and not in this environment'; on bodies, 'That is something I have not witnessed myself.' The witness is testifying to what he was told and what he documented, not to personal observation, and the transcript is unambiguous that he drew that line himself.

Fravor's written statement supplies the other half. He commanded VFA-41 aboard USS Nimitz in November 2004 and describes the Princeton having tracked the objects on Aegis 'for the previous 2 weeks', descending from above 80,000 feet to 20,000 feet, staying for hours, and going 'straight back up'. His closing judgement is about oversight, not phenomenology: 'even Unacknowledged Waived programs have some level of oversight by the appropriate committee members in the House and Senate and this work that is said to be occurring from Whistleblower testimonies should not be exempt.' And the line that indicts the system: 'What is shocking is that the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken, and after a couple of days, it turned into a great story to tell friends.'

The official denial was read into the record by a member reciting AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick's prior testimony that there has been 'no credible evidence thus far of extraterrestrial activity' or of 'off-world technology brought to the attention of the office' - a formulation that is a statement about what reached one office, not about what exists.

What the hearing did not produce is as important as what it did. No contractor was called. No document was subpoenaed. The Committee's own wrap-up release, published the same day, lists its Key Takeaways as poor reporting processes and retaliation against pilots, and quotes Graves estimating that only 'somewhere near five percent' of pilot sightings are reported. Crash retrieval, non-human craft and contractor custody do not appear in the committee's summary of its own hearing.

dossier.whatItIs: A hearing of the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, held 9 September 2025 at 10:00 a.m. in HVC-210, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna with Rep. Jasmine Crockett as ranking member, titled 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection'. The witnesses were Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Senior Chief Petty Officer Alexandro C. Wiggins, George Knapp, Dylan Borland, and minority witness Joe Spielberger of the Project On Government Oversight.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the hearing at which the enquiry stopped being about lights in the sky and became about programme architecture, contracts and custody. Knapp's written testimony placed on the congressional record a detailed account of AAWSAP/BAASS as a prime-contract intelligence programme - fifty cleared investigators, twenty-seven months, a 240,000-case data warehouse still reportedly in agency use, more than a hundred papers never released by DIA - and an account of a negotiated transfer of anomalous material from Lockheed Martin to a private contractor that was agreed and then not completed. Nuccetelli testified that documented, investigated UAP incursions over the National Missile Defense sites at Vandenberg produced records now held by AARO and the FBI, and that a witness was threatened into silence. Wiggins, an active-duty Navy Senior Chief, put multi-sensor Star SAFIRE EO/IR imagery of a transmedium object into the record with time, coordinates and platform. Taken together the hearing establishes that the material, the records and the contracts are locatable - and that the committee could name where they sit without being able to compel their production.
dossier.narrative:
The Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets is a creature of the 119th Congress, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, and it exists because the 2023 and 2024 hearings demonstrated that a standing subcommittee without access to compartments could not move the file. The 9 September 2025 hearing was held in HVC-210, a House Visitor Center room, with five witnesses and written statements posted by the committee.

Jeffrey Nuccetelli, a former Air Force military police officer with sixteen years of active duty, testified to five UAP incidents at Vandenberg Air Force Base between 2003 and 2005 - the home, as his statement notes, of the National Missile Defense Project, during launches described by the National Reconnaissance Office as 'the most important in twenty-five years.' His formulation of the oversight failure is exact: 'Each incident was witnessed by multiple personnel, documented, investigated, and reported up the chain of command. We sent information up, but no guidance came down.' The 14 October 2003 incursion - Boeing contractors reporting 'a massive, glowing red square silently hovering over two missile defense sites' - is the incident Rep. Luna had raised at the 2023 hearing, and Nuccetelli states that 'Official Air Force records documenting it are now held by AARO and the FBI.' That is a custody claim with two named holders. He also testified that after a later incident 'The witness was later threatened and told to kept quiet about the incident, discouraging further reports.'

Alexandro C. Wiggins, an active-duty Navy Senior Chief Petty Officer with roughly twenty-three years of service, gave the hearing its hardest sensor evidence. On 15 February 2023 at approximately 1915 PST, in the W-291 warning area off Southern California, aboard USS Jackson (LCS-6), a self-luminous Tic-Tac-shaped object was observed emerging from the ocean, joined three similar objects, and all four departed simultaneously with no sonic boom and no conventional propulsion signature. The event was recorded from the Combat Information Center on a Star SAFIRE multi-spectral EO/IR system with visible time and location stamps, the objects were held on radar, and reports were made to the Tactical Action Officer. His statement is careful about what the data does and does not show, and notes an approximate altitude reference of about 22,000 feet reflected in CIC operator conversation.

George Knapp's written testimony is the document that makes this hearing structurally important. He describes AAWSAP as conceived by DIA's Dr. James Lacatski and a colleague, funded through Senator Harry Reid and two other senior senators, and contracted to Robert Bigelow's BAASS, which 'managed to recruit and hire fifty full-time investigators for BAASS, most of them former military or law enforcement, and all of whom were able to qualify for top-secret security clearances.' In twenty-seven months the programme produced 'more than three dozen preliminary reports (DIRDs)' and 'compiled the largest known UFO database - or rather data warehouse - consisting of more than 240,000 case files obtained from multiple other collections, including files from other governments.' That warehouse 'was designed and overseen by Dr. Jacques Vallee and has reportedly been used by U.S. agencies up to the present date.' The programme also produced 'more than 100 highly detailed papers', of which 'None of these 100-plus reports have been released by DIA, though a few have been leaked.'

Knapp then puts two custody claims on the record. First, Lacatski's 2023 statement during Kona Blue discussions with a US senator and an undersecretary of the Department of Homeland Security that 'the U.S. is in possession of a craft of unknown origin and had successfully gained access to its interior', described as having 'a streamlined configuration suitable for aerodynamic flight but no intakes, exhaust, wings, or control surfaces.' Second, and more concrete: 'I have confirmed that Bigelow and a trusted colleague met with and negotiated with a senior executive at Lockheed and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that Lockheed was safeguarding at a facility in California. A source who was in the room for that discussion has confirmed this.' The material 'contained no unknown element, no unobtanium, but its composition suggested it had been crafted in a zero-gravity environment.' And then: 'The agreement was not completed.'

Knapp also notes, almost in passing, a fact that matters for how this file is now being worked: 'Mr. Grusch now works for Representative Burlison as an advisor on these matters.' The 2023 whistleblower is now congressional staff support on the same subject.

The Russian half of Knapp's testimony - Ministry of Defence documents from his 1993 and 1996 Moscow visits, Colonel Boris Sokolov's decade-long standing collection order 1978-1988, General Igor Maltsev's standing order to disengage, the October 1982 Ukraine missile base incident in which launch displays illuminated and could not be shut down - is presented as material already handed to AAWSAP and BAASS for analysis, with the resulting report 'included in one of those unreleased papers submitted to DIA and still bottled up there.'

The minority witness, Joe Spielberger of the Project On Government Oversight, was there for whistleblower protection rather than phenomena, which is the correct read of the hearing's title. The Task Force's theory is that the bottleneck is not evidence but the legal exposure of the people who hold it.

dossier.whatItIs: A twelve-page document that Michael Shellenberger delivered to Congress on the morning of 13 November 2024 and that Rep. Nancy Mace moved into the Congressional Record from the dais during the House Oversight Committee hearing 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Exposing the Truth'. Its first section describes an unacknowledged special access program named Immaculate Constellation; its second section concerns United States Government imagery intelligence. It is listed in the hearing's Index of Documents as 'Report, Pentagon, "Immaculate Constellation"; submitted by Rep. Mace.'
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only artefact in the entire public record that purports to be an internal description of a UAP parent compartment, and a chairwoman of a House committee put it into the Congressional Record while the Department of Defense was on record saying it has no record of the programme it names. The document is therefore a test case for the whole disclosure machinery: a congressional committee can receive, distribute to every member on the dais, and formally enter a document about an unacknowledged SAP, and nothing follows. No agency was compelled to search for it, no author was subpoenaed, no classification review was triggered, and no executive branch office has addressed its contents. It is the disclosure mechanism working exactly as designed and producing exactly nothing.
dossier.narrative:
The document arrived on the morning of the hearing. Rep. Mace flagged it in her opening remarks before the witnesses were sworn: 'there is a document that will be entered into the congressional record today. Mr. Tim Burchett from Tennessee has this document, and we just distributed it to every Member up here on the dais, this document. But this is going to be the original document from the Pentagon about Immaculate Constellation that Michael Shellenberger delivered to Congress today.' She then characterised it: '12 pages about this unacknowledged special access program that your government says does not exist.'

Later in the hearing, after the last of the opening statements, she performed the formal act: 'Committee staff asked me to go ahead, and I will do it, to enter into the Congressional Record this 12-page document that Michael Shellenberger brought today that describes the Immaculate Constellation government program. So, we will do that now. Every Member up here has a copy of it.' She then described its structure on the record: 'The first section talks about the unacknowledged special access program called Immaculate Constellation, and the second section about USG imagery intelligence.' She added the FISA warning she had just received from Rep. Luna, and closed with 'But, without objection, entered into the record.'

The printed hearing record's Index of Documents lists it as 'Report, Pentagon, "Immaculate Constellation"; submitted by Rep. Mace', alongside a Mellon hearing letter submitted by Mace, documents related to UAPs submitted by Burchett, and Questions for the Record to Elizondo, Gallaudet, Shellenberger and Gold submitted by Burlison. The record states that 'The documents listed above are available at: docs.house.gov.'

The contents, as read into the record by Shellenberger in his oral statement and set out at greater length in his written testimony, are consistent between the two. The report describes a parent USAP consolidating UAP observations from tasked and untasked collection platforms; a holdings profile of high-quality IMINT and MASINT from low Earth orbit, the upper atmosphere, aviation altitudes and maritime environments; a shape taxonomy of spheres and orbs, discs and saucers, ovals and tic-tacs, triangles, boomerang and arrowhead forms and irregular or organic shapes; and seven categories of evidence. The written testimony says the report 'describes in detail various UAP sightings collected by technical assets and US military personnel', and that the underlying material sits in defence HUMINT databases 'accessible to the Intelligence Community'.

Two incident descriptions are quoted directly from the report in the written testimony. The F-22 encounter: 'The F-22 broke trajectory and attempted to evade but was intercepted and boxed in by approximately 3-6 UAPs', with one object holding station off the cockpit through multiple evasive manoeuvres before the aircraft 'was forced out of the mission area under the escort of the UAP formation.' And the carrier deck event, in which a small orange-red sphere descended from high altitude to within 100-200 yards directly above the flight deck of a CVN.

The evidentiary character of the document is worth stating plainly, because the argument does not need it inflated. It is an anonymous report, delivered by a journalist, whose author Shellenberger says he knows and will not name. Under questioning from Rep. Higgins he confirmed 'I do' when asked whether he knew the author, and when pressed on the author's sources referred back to the report itself. He offered one internal check: that when he compared its cases against publicly known cases he 'did not find it based on existing cases; it was new cases for me', which he presented as an argument against circular reporting. That is a weak check, and he said so in effect by presenting it as the only one he could make.

What gives the document its standing is not its provenance but its position. It sits in the Congressional Record. It was distributed to every member on the dais of a House committee. It names a compartment. And the executive branch response to it, before and since, has been a single sentence from a public affairs office - Sue Gough's statement that 'The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called "IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION"' - which addresses records holdings and not existence, and which was itself printed in the witness's own testimony rather than issued in response to the congressional entry.

Since 13 November 2024 the document has been followed by nothing. No agency has confirmed conducting a search. No committee has published a referral. No classification authority has asserted that the document is classified, which would be the ordinary response to an authentic Pentagon report on an unacknowledged SAP appearing in a public hearing room; nor has any authority asserted that it is a forgery, which would be the ordinary response to a fabrication. That double silence is the most interesting fact about the artefact. The disclosure machinery accepted the document and then had nowhere to put it, because the mechanism Congress built in 2023 - a records collection administered by the agencies that hold the records - has no procedure for a document that arrives from outside the agencies and describes a compartment the agencies say they cannot find.

Rep. Mace described the document's structure on the record: 'The first section talks about the unacknowledged special access program called Immaculate Constellation, and the second section about USG imagery intelligence.'

His written testimony states that 'The whistleblower's report includes seven categories of evidence' and that it 'describes in detail various UAP sightings collected by technical assets and US military personnel.'

Asked what evidence substantiated the programme's existence, Shellenberger said the members had the report in front of them and added: 'I checked the report, and I did not find it based on existing cases; it was new cases for me ... that answered for me that it was not obviously circular reporting.'
