dossier.whatItIs: To The Stars Academy of Arts and Science Inc. was a Delaware public benefit corporation incorporated in 2017 and registered with the SEC under Commission File Number 024-10728, CIK 1710274, EIN 82-0601064. Its directors were Tom DeLonge, former CIA Directorate of Operations officer Jim Semivan, and physicist Harold Puthoff; Lockheed Skunk Works veteran Steve Justice and former Pentagon official Luis Elizondo were listed as significant employees. It raised money through a Regulation A offering, hosted the first officially released US military UAP videos, and signed a research agreement with the US Army before winding down its aerospace work and reverting to entertainment as To The Stars Inc.
dossier.whyImplicated: TTSA matters to this map not as a research institution but as a legal vehicle. For roughly three years it was the corporate person through which men carrying intelligence, special-access and black-aerospace careers could act in public, hold material, sign agreements with the government, and speak to Congress and the press without a government employer's prepublication apparatus sitting on top of every sentence. Its SEC filings are the single richest primary record on this board of who those people were, what clearances and career histories they carried, and what the venture was actually organised to do. In October 2019 it converted that standing into a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command covering 'material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage' - a government laboratory relationship with a private company that held claimed anomalous material. AARO's own history records the same personnel network attempting to reconstitute the AAWSAP effort inside the Department of Homeland Security as the prospective special access programme KONA BLUE.
dossier.narrative:
To The Stars Academy is the most thoroughly documented entity on this board, for a reason that has nothing to do with UAP: it sold securities. A company that offers stock under Regulation A must file with the SEC, and the filings are public, dated, signed and auditable. The FY2017 Form 1-K is therefore the closest thing this subject has to a sworn organisational chart.

What it shows is a very small company with a very unusual staff. Officers and directors were Tom DeLonge as president and interim chief executive; Jim Semivan as vice president of operations and director; and Harold E. Puthoff as vice president of science and technology and director. The filing states that Semivan 'retired from the Central Intelligence Agency's Directorate of Operations after 25 years working as an operations officer both overseas and domestically,' that he 'was a member of the CIA's Senior Intelligence Service,' and that he 'currently holds Top Secret Clearances.' It states that Puthoff is president and chief executive of EarthTech International and director of the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin. Two significant employees are listed: Steve Justice, Director of Advanced Programs and Technology, part-time at twenty hours a week, whose industry background the filing ties to the Lockheed organisation 'known as the "Skunk Works"'; and Luis Elizondo, Chief of Security and Special Programs, full-time, described as a career intelligence officer. As of 31 December 2017 the company had eleven employees.

The financial picture in the same filing is stark. Revenues for 2017 were $1,376,215 against cost of revenues of $750,932, producing gross profit of $625,283 - essentially a merchandise and music business. The net loss for 2017 was $30,665,436, against $422,670 the prior year, almost entirely non-cash stock compensation. Gravity Holdings LLC, whose sole member is the DeLonge Family Trust, held 60,000,000 Class A shares, 85.7 per cent of the class. This was not a research budget. It was a capital structure wrapped around a founder and a small group of named individuals.

What the company did with that structure is the part that belongs on this map. It became, as the filing puts it, 'the very first company to obtain official U.S. Government footage of unidentified aerial phenomena ("UAP") that had gone through the declassification process and been approved for public release,' publishing the footage through its online Community of Interest. The videos that entered the mainstream through the New York Times in December 2017 - the material now known as FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast - reached the public through a private securities issuer, not through a Pentagon press release. That routing is itself a finding. A declassification review was completed and the product was handed to a company in which a serving-until-recently Pentagon official was chief of security and special programs.

On 17 October 2019 TTSA announced a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command 'to advance TTSA's materiel and technology innovations in order to develop enhanced capabilities for Army ground vehicles.' The announcement described the technology set as leveraging 'developments in material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage,' and set out the exchange: 'TTSA will share its discoveries with Ground Vehicle System Center (GVSC) and Ground Vehicle Survivability and Protection (GVSP) and the U.S. Army shall provide laboratories, expertise, support, and resources to help characterize the technologies and its applications.' Dr Joseph Cannon of US Army Futures Command called the partnership 'an exciting, non-traditional source for novel materials and transformational technologies.' Steve Justice, by then TTSA's chief operating officer and aerospace division director, said the agreement brought 'additional, critically important expertise that is necessary to advance the state-of-the-art in both our near and long-term technology areas of study.'

Read against the rest of this board, the CRADA is the important document. A private company holding material it described as anomalous obtained access to Army laboratories to characterise it, under an instrument that is not a procurement contract and does not require the government to pay. A CRADA moves capability and data across the government-private boundary in both directions with far less contractual and oversight furniture than a prime contract, and it does so without a competitive solicitation. Whether or not anything anomalous was ever in those laboratories, the mechanism is precisely the kind of low-visibility government-private research channel this board is built to map.

The network did not begin with TTSA and did not end with it. AARO's Historical Record Report records that after AAWSAP was terminated, 'its supporters unsuccessfully attempted to convince DHS to support a new version of this effort dubbed KONA BLUE,' which AARO characterises as 'a UAP-related Prospective Special Access Program (PSAP) called KONA BLUE that was proposed to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and supported by individuals who believed the USG was hiding off-world technology,' and which 'was never approved by DHS.' The same people, in sequence: a DIA contract, a proposed DHS special access programme, a Delaware public benefit corporation, a congressional hearing.

Elizondo, Christopher Mellon and Justice departed in December 2020, the aerospace and materials work wound down, and the entity renamed itself To The Stars Inc. and returned to entertainment. What it leaves behind is a documentary trail that is unusually hard to argue with, because it was filed under penalty of securities law: names, ages, clearances, prior employers, share counts, losses, and an executed agreement with a US Army laboratory command.

dossier.whatItIs: The MITRE Corporation is a private not-for-profit spun out of MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1958 that operates exclusively as a manager of federally funded research and development centers. It runs six FFRDCs on behalf of the Department of Defense, the Federal Aviation Administration, Treasury and the IRS, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Health and Human Services, and NIST. It is headquartered in McLean, Virginia, and also provides the administrative home for JASON, the government's standing outside scientific advisory panel.
dossier.whyImplicated: MITRE is on this map because of the legal mechanism it embodies, not because a witness has named it as a custodian of material. An FFRDC is granted, by regulation, access to government and contractor data 'beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship' - including sensitive and proprietary data, installations, equipment and real property - and its sponsoring agreement gives the sponsor's Executive Agent approval authority over the classification, publication and distribution of its output. That combination produces a private organisation holding federal program records under a disclosure obligation that runs to a sponsoring agency rather than to Congress or to the public, and whose corporate files are not agency records for FOIA purposes. The DHS sponsoring agreement goes further: MITRE's own staff sign non-disclosure agreements that expressly preserve the right to report substantial violations of law to Congress, but subcontractors and consultants are required to sign the same NDA with that whistleblower carve-back removed. On 22 May 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison put this exact structure in writing, telling MITRE that FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records' and demanding a search back to 1 January 1930.
dossier.narrative:
MITRE occupies a category that exists nowhere else in the federal enterprise. It manufactures nothing, competes for nothing, and sells nothing. It exists to hold institutional memory and technical judgement on behalf of government sponsors, and the Federal Acquisition Regulation builds that role out of a single privilege: an FFRDC 'has access, beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship, to Government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary data, and to employees and installations equipment and real property.' That sentence, FAR 35.017(a)(2), is the load-bearing beam of this dossier. Everything a prime contractor knows about its own black programmes, and everything the government knows about the prime, can lawfully sit inside the FFRDC that sits between them.

MITRE currently operates six FFRDCs: the National Security Engineering Center for DoD; the Center for Advanced Aviation System Development for the FAA; the Center for Enterprise Modernization for Treasury and the IRS, co-sponsored by Veterans Affairs, the Social Security Administration and Commerce; the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute for DHS; the Health FFRDC for HHS; and the National Cybersecurity FFRDC for NIST. Its own fact sheet notes there are only forty-two FFRDCs in total and that operating six of them is 'a high honor.' The relevant point for this board is not prestige but coverage: one nonprofit sits inside the defence establishment, the intelligence-adjacent national security enterprise, and the civil aviation regulator that owns the primary radar picture of American airspace.

The governing document that shows how this works in practice is the FY2009 sponsoring agreement between DHS and MITRE for HS SEDI, signed by MITRE's president and by the Acting Under Secretary for Science and Technology on 13 March 2009. It is worth reading as a specification for exactly the kind of custody problem this board is mapping. Section 3 states that SEDI's work 'will often require privileged access to information, including sensitive Government information and industry proprietary data not normally available to non-Government organizations.' Section 5(h) obliges the sponsors to 'provide access to classified and sensitive data, facilities, plans and related information, including proprietary data.' Section 6(c)(9) records the routine practice: 'Ordinarily, sponsors release classified, privileged, no-contractor, and other sensitive material directly to SEDI.' Section 5(a) states plainly that 'The SEDI will work on many classified and highly sensitive projects.'

Then the agreement closes the loop on disclosure. Section 6(b)(9) gives the DHS Executive Agent authority to review and approve 'the classification, publication, and distribution of SEDI publications.' Section 9(g) defines 'Privileged Information' so broadly that it captures every deliverable, note, lab record, test result and analysis MITRE produces for the sponsor, and forbids disclosure except as required by law or 'as expressly authorized in writing by the DHS Executive Agent.' Section 9(g)(2) then carves back the whistleblower statutes, stating that 'Signing this Agreement does not bar disclosures to Congress or to an authorized official of an executive agency or the Department of Justice that are essential to reporting a substantial violation of law.' That is the protective clause. And Section 5(j)(iv) requires MITRE to make every subcontractor and consultant sign a non-disclosure agreement containing the Section 9(g) terms 'with the exception of Section 9(g)(2).' The people at the outer edge of the work - the ones brought in for specialised expertise MITRE does not hold in-house - are contractually bound by the secrecy terms without the clause that preserves their right to tell Congress.

This is the structural argument, and on 22 May 2026 a member of Congress made it out loud. Rep. Eric Burlison, of the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, sent a ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests to MITRE's president Mark Peters and its general counsel Christopher Land. The relevant time period is 'January 1, 1930, to the present.' The definitions section reaches every MITRE-operated FFRDC, every subcontractor, and any record 'described, coded, compartmented, or euphemized as involving UAP, UFO, USO, transmedium craft, advanced aerospace threat, technology of unknown origin, non-human intelligence, legacy crash retrieval, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, recovered vehicle, recovered material, biological material, or equivalent terms.'

The interrogatories are targeted at exactly the mechanism described above. Section III demands identification of every Special Access Program, Controlled Access Program, Alternative Compensatory Control Measure, Managed-Need-To-Know codeword and DOE SIGMA category MITRE participated in or supported in connection with UAP records, and asks whether each 'was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.' It asks MITRE to identify any classification guide, NDA, access roster or sponsor communication that instructed personnel to avoid using the terms UAP, UFO, crash retrieval or reverse engineering in records. Section VIII asks for every NDA or indoctrination instrument 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations that restricted MITRE personnel from reporting UAP-related matters to Congress.' Section IX asks MITRE to identify any UAP-related work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems or Bigelow Aerospace. Section X asks whether responsive funding was routed through a cover programme 'whose public description differed materially from the responsive work performed.' The letter warns that concealment or destruction may implicate 18 U.S.C. sections 1001, 1505, 1512, 1519 and 2071.

MITRE's reply, given to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was a single sentence from a spokesperson: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' That answer is not evasive so much as accurate. It restates the architecture the letter was written to expose. An FFRDC's disclosure obligation runs to its sponsor. Congress asks MITRE; MITRE asks the sponsor; the sponsor is the same authority that classified the work. What the record does not contain, as of this writing, is the certification of search methodology, the records-location index, the preservation hold, or any production - all of which the letter demanded on 30- and 45-day clocks.

GAO/NSIAD-95-187 — Results of a Search for Records Concerning the 1947 Crash Near Roswell
Roswell Incident

dossier.whatItIs: On 8 July 1947 the Roswell Army Air Field public information office announced that personnel of the 509th Bomb Group had recovered a crashed "flying disc" on a ranch in the Roswell region. The following day the Commanding General of Eighth Air Force at Fort Worth announced the object was a radar-tracking weather balloon. The Air Force issued two further explanations decades later: a 1994 report attributing the debris to a Project MOGUL balloon train, and a 1997 report attributing reports of "alien bodies" to anthropomorphic test dummies and to two later aircraft and balloon mishaps.
dossier.whyImplicated: The argument here is not about what fell. It is about the file. When the General Accounting Office audited the record in 1994-95 at the request of Rep. Steven Schiff, it found that Roswell Army Air Field's administrative records for March 1945 through December 1949 and its outgoing messages for October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed, and that "the document disposition form does not indicate what organization or person destroyed the records and when or under what authority." The unit records of the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation), the unit that would have cordoned any site, could not be shown ever to have been retired to a records depository at all. Only two documents originating in 1947 survived the search. The FBI teletype that survives states the recovered object was being sent to Wright Field for examination, and GAO's review of Air Materiel Command records for 1947 to 1950 found nothing about the receipt or examination of any Roswell debris. A government that recovered a weather balloon does not lose four years of a bomb group's message traffic without a disposal authority, and does not fail to log the arrival of the item at the laboratory it says received it.
dossier.narrative:
Roswell is the origin node of the entire concealment argument, and the strongest evidence for it is not testimony. It is an audit report signed by a GAO director in 1995.

The sequence of public statements is short and well documented. On 8 July 1947 the RAAF public information office reported the recovery of a "flying disc," credited to personnel of the 509th Bomb Group. Within a day the story was replaced: Eighth Air Force at Fort Worth announced a crashed radar-tracking balloon. The July 1947 combined history report of the 509th Bomb Group and RAAF, one of only two surviving 1947 documents, records that the public information office "was kept quite busy . . . answering inquiries on the 'flying disc,' which was reported to be in [the] possession of the 509th Bomb Group. The object turned out to be a radar tracking balloon." The commanding officer certified by signature that the report was a complete and accurate account of RAAF activities for that month. The second surviving document is an FBI teletype from the Dallas field office dated 8 July 1947, whose authenticity an FBI spokesperson confirmed to GAO, reporting that an Eighth Air Force headquarters official had telephoned to describe the recovery near Roswell of "a hexagonal-shaped disc suspended from a large balloon by cable," and that "the disc and balloon were being sent to Wright Field . . . for examination."

That is the entire 1947 documentary record. Everything else was gone by the time anyone looked.

GAO looked hard. Its team worked from March 1994 to June 1995 across the National Archives in Washington and at College Park, the records center at Suitland, the National Personnel Records Center in St. Louis, the Air Force Safety Agency at Kirtland, the Air Force History Support Office at Bolling, NSA at Fort Meade, the Army Central Security Facility, CIA at Langley, FBI headquarters and elsewhere, and queried the National Security Council, the Office of Science and Technology Policy, the Department of Energy, the FBI, DOD and CIA in writing. It reviewed classified material. What it reported was a hole shaped exactly like the event.

The Chief Archivist of the National Personnel Records Center documented for GAO that RAAF records covering finance and accounting, supplies, buildings and grounds and other general administrative matters from March 1945 through December 1949, together with RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949, had been destroyed, and that "the document disposition form did not properly indicate the authority under which the disposal action was taken." GAO's flat summary sentence is the one that matters: "although some of the records concerning Roswell activities had been destroyed, there was no information available regarding when or under what authority the records were destroyed." The Chief Archivist offered the mitigating view that many Air Force organizational records of that period were destroyed without a disposition citation, and GAO noted that its own review of the destruction forms for RAAF's 1950 outgoing messages supported that view. That is a fair caveat and it is in the record. It does not restore the messages.

A separate gap sits underneath it. GAO specifically sought the records of the military units assigned to RAAF in 1947 - the 509th Bomb Group, the 1st Air Transport Unit, the 427th Army Air Force Base Unit, and the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation). Disposition forms from St. Louis show a Walker Air Force Base records officer transferring the first three unit histories to the Army's Kansas City depository in 1953. Of the fourth, GAO wrote: "We could not locate any documentation indicating that records of the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) were ever retired to the National Personnel Records Center or its predecessor depositories." The military police company is the unit that secures a crash site. Its paper is the only unit paper that does not exist.

The third gap closes the loop. Because the surviving FBI teletype says the material went to Wright Field, GAO tried to find the regulation governing how such debris should be handled and reported: "We were unable to locate any applicable regulation." It then reviewed Air Materiel Command records at Wright Field from 1947 to 1950 and "found no records mentioning the Roswell crash or the examination by Air Materiel Command personnel of any debris recovered from the crash." The item arrives nowhere. GAO also established that in 1947 Army regulations required air accident reports to be maintained permanently, that four air accidents were reported in New Mexico in July 1947 and all occurred after 8 July involving military aircraft, and that Air Force officials said no requirement existed to report a weather balloon crash - which is a clean explanation for the absence of an accident report and no explanation at all for the absence of the message traffic.

CIA's answer is its own artifact. In March 1995 the Agency's Executive Director told GAO that earlier UFO record searches had produced nothing on Roswell but that "it was unclear whether the CIA had ever conducted a search for records specifically relating to Roswell," and ordered one. On 30 May 1995 he reported that a search on the term "Roswell, New Mexico" across all CIA databases produced no documents. Forty-eight years after the event and one year into a congressional audit, the Agency was not sure it had ever looked.

The two Air Force reports arrived on either side of the GAO audit and moved the explanation twice. The 1994 report, announced by Secretary of the Air Force Sheila Widnall on 8 September 1994, concluded that the most likely source of the recovered wreckage was a Project MOGUL balloon train, a then-classified acoustic effort to detect Soviet nuclear tests; DOD told GAO that this report "represents the extent of DOD records or information concerning the Roswell crash." The 1997 report, The Roswell Report: Case Closed, addressed the body reports and concluded that "Air Force activities which occurred over a period of many years have been consolidated and are now represented to have occurred in two or three days in July 1947," that the "aliens" were anthropomorphic test dummies carried aloft by high-altitude balloons, and that claims of bodies at the RAAF hospital most likely combine a 1956 KC-97 accident that killed eleven airmen and a 1959 manned balloon mishap that injured two pilots. The dummy drops and both mishaps postdate July 1947 by between seven and twelve years. The Air Force's answer to that is that witness memory compressed the decade. It is a testable claim and it is on the record under signature, which is what makes it useful here.

claims.text: GAO found that RAAF administrative records from March 1945 through December 1949 and RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949 were destroyed, and that "the document disposition form does not indicate what organization or person destroyed the records and when or under what authority the records were destroyed."
GAO's search of federal holdings yielded only two records originating in 1947: the July 1947 combined history report of the 509th Bomb Group and RAAF, and an FBI teletype dated 8 July 1947.

GAO reported: "We could not locate any documentation indicating that records of the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) were ever retired to the National Personnel Records Center or its predecessor depositories."

The 8 July 1947 FBI teletype, whose authenticity an FBI spokesperson confirmed to GAO, states that an Eighth Air Force headquarters official reported the recovery near Roswell of a hexagonal-shaped disc suspended from a large balloon by cable, and that the disc and balloon "were being sent to Wright Field . . . for examination."

GAO reviewed Air Materiel Command (Wright Field) records from 1947 to 1950 and "found no records mentioning the Roswell crash or the examination by Air Materiel Command personnel of any debris recovered from the crash."
GAO attempted to identify the military regulations governing the handling of such debris and reported: "We were unable to locate any applicable regulation."

In March 1995 the CIA Executive Director told GAO it was "unclear whether the CIA had ever conducted a search for records specifically relating to Roswell" and ordered one; on 30 May 1995 he reported that a search on "Roswell, New Mexico" across all CIA databases produced no documents.

GAO stated in its scope and methodology section: "Our search of government records was complicated by the fact that some records we wanted to review were missing and there was not always an explanation."

GAO found that in 1947 Army regulations required air accident reports to be maintained permanently, that no military service filed a report on the Roswell incident, and that Air Force officials stated there was no requirement to prepare a report on the crash of a weather balloon.

DOD informed GAO that the July 1994 Report of Air Force Research Regarding the Roswell Incident "represents the extent of DOD records or information concerning the Roswell crash," and that report concluded the most likely source of the wreckage was one of the Project MOGUL balloon trains.

The Air Force's 1997 report The Roswell Report: Case Closed concludes that "Air Force activities which occurred over a period of many years have been consolidated and are now represented to have occurred in two or three days in July 1947," that reported "aliens" were anthropomorphic test dummies carried by high-altitude balloons, and that body claims at the RAAF hospital most likely combine a 1956 KC-97 accident killing eleven airmen and a 1959 manned balloon mishap injuring two pilots.

dossier.denialPosture: Three official positions exist, each dated and attributable: Eighth Air Force, 9 July 1947, a radar-tracking weather balloon; the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force, 8 September 1994 under Secretary Sheila Widnall, a Project MOGUL balloon train; and Headquarters USAF, 24 June 1997, anthropomorphic test dummies plus a 1956 aircraft accident and a 1959 balloon mishap. The 1994 and 1997 reports also assert that Air Force research "did not locate or develop any information that the 'Roswell Incident' was a UFO event nor was there any indication of a 'cover-up' by the Government." No official statement has ever explained the destruction of the 1945-1949 RAAF administrative and message files without a disposition authority.
openQuestions: Who destroyed the RAAF administrative records and outgoing messages, when, and under what authority? GAO could not answer this and no agency has since.
Where are the records of the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation), and were they ever accessioned anywhere?
If the FBI teletype is correct that the material went to Wright Field, why do Air Materiel Command files for 1947-1950 contain no receipt, examination or disposition entry?
The July 1947 RAAF press release itself, as distributed, has not been located in primary form in the federal record; only the 509th unit history's paraphrase and press accounts survive.

The so-called Ramey memo - the sheet of paper visible in the 8 July 1947 Fort Worth press photographs - has no authoritative government transcription. Any reading of it remains an interpretive claim and is deliberately excluded from the claims above.

Whether any 1947 material relating to Roswell exists in still-classified compartmented series that GAO's 1994-95 access did not reach; GAO reviewed classified holdings but its access was not unlimited and it did not audit special access programs.

dossier.whatItIs: The Sol Foundation is a private non-profit co-founded by Stanford pathology professor Garry Nolan and anthropologist Peter Skafish that describes its work as science, policy and public education for what it calls the post-UAP world. It runs observational and analytical research projects, publishes a numbered white-paper and policy-briefing series, and holds an annual conference. In June 2026 five people connected to it - both co-founders, a senior adviser, an advisory board member and its production lead - were named to the US government's UAP Science Advisory Council.
dossier.whyImplicated: Sol is the institution that converted the private technical layer into a policy actor with standing inside government. Its published output is not popular advocacy; it is a policy programme aimed squarely at the concealment mechanism, including a November 2024 paper by its own executive director on executive-branch UAP secrecy and the harm to Congress, a May 2025 paper by retired Colonel Karl Nell calling for US government disclosure, and an April 2026 briefing by its senior legislative affairs officer - a 37-year Senate Armed Services Committee staffer - proposing a whistleblower restitution fund to incentivise disclosures to Congress. Within under three years of formation, that programme placed a plurality of the members of the first standing outside scientific advisory body the US government has convened on this subject. The single largest gap in the Sol record is that it names no donors, and the board treats an unfunded map of a funding question as an open problem rather than a settled one.
dossier.narrative:
The Sol Foundation is the closest thing the modern disclosure effort has to a think tank, and the useful way to read it is by its bibliography rather than its press. Its publication series is numbered, dated and authored, and the sequence tells you what the organisation actually decided to work on.

The first tranche in 2024 was scoping work. Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, US Navy retired, published 'Beneath the Surface: We May Learn More about UAP by Looking in the Ocean' in March 2024, arguing that transmedium UAP and unidentified submersible objects are the overlooked domain. The foundation itself published 'UAP in Crowded Skies' in the same month and 'Anomalous Health Threats: Health Security Considerations for UAP' in July. Helen McCaw wrote on UK policy implications in May 2024. Paul Thigpen wrote on the Catholic Church's likely response in July.

Then in November 2024 Peter Skafish, the foundation's executive director and co-founder, published 'The Prospect of Executive Branch Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Secrecy: The Harm to Congress and Potential Remedies.' That is the pivot. The subject is no longer whether UAP are anomalous; it is whether an executive-branch secrecy regime has concealed decades of knowledge, research programmes and potentially retrieved technologies from Congress itself, and what remedies exist. In May 2025 the series published Colonel Karl E. Nell, retired, on 'The UFO Enigma: A Call for US Government Disclosure,' framed around the effort to revive the UAP Disclosure Act.

By 2026 the series had become numbered Science and Policy Briefings and had acquired an author who is the point of the whole exercise. Briefing No. 2, April 2026, is 'UAP Whistleblower Restitution Fund Would Incentivize Disclosures to Congress,' by Kirk McConnell. McConnell is Sol's senior legislative affairs officer and spent thirty-seven years on the staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee. The paper's premise is stated at the top: individuals considering disclosing information about classified executive-branch UAP programmes to Congress face significant retaliation, including immediate loss of livelihood, and several senators have said so. That is a former SASC staffer, writing under a foundation's imprint, designing a financial instrument to overcome the deterrent that the special-access architecture places on contractor and government employees who might talk to his old committee. Briefings No. 1 and No. 3, both by Marik von Rennenkampff, cover Beatriz Villarroel's pre-satellite-era night-sky plate work and what the foundation describes as the first peer-reviewed scientific analysis of possible UAP materials, involving Garry Nolan.

That combination - a Stanford immunologist doing materials and biological analysis, a career Senate Armed Services staffer doing legislative design, an anthropologist doing the theory of secrecy - is why Sol belongs on this map. It is not a UFO group. It is a small institution that identified the mechanism, staffed against it, and published a remedy.

The consequence arrived in June 2026. Following what the foundation calls 'historic releases of government records about UAP encounters,' the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, with the support of the FBI, announced a UAP Science Advisory Council led by Avi Loeb, who sits on Sol's own advisory board. The foundation's announcement states that among the fourteen scientists and experts named were Sol co-founders Garry Nolan and Peter Skafish; Sol senior adviser Tim Gallaudet; and Sol advisory board member Jacob Haqq-Misra. Ross Howard, who leads production for the foundation, would lead communications for the council. The council reports to a higher-level UAP Governance Board, 'an interagency body coordinating across military, law enforcement, and intelligence community agencies,' and 'All data shared with the council will be unclassified.' The foundation's own framing is unambiguous about what it thinks happened: 'The appointment of Sol's co-founders, Admiral (ret.) Gallaudet and Dr. Jacob Haqq-Misra to the government's scientific advisory body is a fulfillment of its founding mission. Sol can now share its insight to the highest levels of government deliberation about disclosure, amplifying our impact.'

Two things about that are worth holding separately. The first is a genuine institutional achievement: a private foundation went from formation to supplying a plurality of the government's outside scientific advisers on this subject in under three years. The second is a caution the board should apply without softening it: the council those people joined is, on the government's own description, unclassified-only. A body with no access to classified material cannot examine recovered material, cannot audit a carve-out special access programme, and cannot compel anything. Sol's own executive director wrote the paper explaining exactly why that matters. The organisation that best articulated the executive-branch secrecy problem has now placed its people inside a body that has been constituted on the far side of the secrecy line.

The last thing to say about Sol is the thing it does not say about itself. Its site solicits membership and donations. It names no donors, no foundations and no corporate supporters. For an entity on a board whose organising question is who pays, that is the largest single documentary gap in its record, and it is not resolved by anything published as of this writing. There is also a small unresolved inconsistency in its own account of its founding date - the June 2026 announcement says the foundation 'was established in 2023,' which does not match every version the organisation has published.

dossier.whatItIs: Lockheed Martin Corporation is the largest single recipient of United States defense contract obligations, formed by the 1995 merger of Lockheed and Martin Marietta. It operates cleared facilities accredited for Special Access Program work and runs the Advanced Development Programs organisation, the Skunk Works, which has built the U-2, SR-71 and F-117 among other classified aircraft. It is the only corporation named on the record, by a sworn witness in a congressional hearing, as a holder of recovered non-terrestrial material.
dossier.whyImplicated: Lockheed Martin sits at the intersection of the two conditions this board treats as necessary for a legacy programme to survive without congressional visibility: a company with the industrial capacity to store and work on recovered material, and a legal regime that can lift normal industrial security oversight off it. Under 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) the Director of DCSA is relieved of National Industrial Security Program oversight for DoD special access programs whenever the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves a carve-out provision. Under DoD Directive 5205.07, no contractor employee or consultant may provide SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff without the approval of the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. Two sworn witnesses - George Knapp in September 2025 and Luis Elizondo in November 2024 - have testified to a specific, dated, blocked transaction in which material collected in the 1950s and held at a California facility was to move from a corporation to Bigelow's BAASS, and did not. Lockheed Martin has issued no public rebuttal of that sworn testimony.
dossier.narrative:
The Lockheed Martin allegation is unusual on this board because it is the one that has been made under oath, in a hearing room, with a company name attached. On 9 September 2025, before the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, George Knapp told the committee: 'It has been widely reported and suspected that Lockheed Martin is one of the contractors - the defense contractors, that has held this stuff, stored it away in secrecy, and tried to figure out how it works.' He then went further and put his own reporting on the record: 'I have confirmed on the record that Robert Bigelow and a trusted colleague from AAWSAP met with and negotiated with senior executives at Lockheed Martin and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow's company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that had been stashed away and protected at a facility in California. That material was not made here.' Later in the same hearing Rep. Tim Burchett asked which corporations hold the material. Knapp answered: 'Well, one of them is Lockheed.' He added a line that is, for the purposes of this map, more revealing than the accusation itself: 'I am not saying Lockheed's the bad guys. They are doing what they were asked to do. ... They have lied about this because that is what they are supposed to do.'

Ten months earlier, on 13 November 2024, Luis Elizondo had testified to the same transaction from inside the government side of it. Asked by Rep. Burlison whether the government or defence contractors possess technology, Elizondo said one reason his predecessor programme AAWSAP was trying to collect material of unknown origin was that 'there was an aerospace contract company that requested to divest itself of the material ... that was collected in the 1950s. Unfortunately, that did not actually occur.' Burlison then put the Christopher Sharp reporting to him directly - a transfer between Lockheed Martin, Bigelow Aerospace, and a CIA block - and Elizondo answered: 'What I can say is that it was blocked. Why it was blocked, I can only surmise. I was part of some conversations later on with some of those contract personnel where they had told all of us that is accurate.' He described the missing instrument: 'What we required was a memo from the Secretary of the Air Force in order to make that complete, and that never occurred.'

The official record does not name the company, but it does record the allegation. AARO's Historical Record Report, Volume I, logs an interviewee claim that an organisation 'was in possession of off-world material in 2009 and 2010,' that a separate interviewee 'participated in negotiations to return the material to the USG,' and that 'a former named senior CIA official quashed the proposal to remove the material from the corporation.' A separate entry logs a claim that an organisation held twelve spacecraft recovered from crash events prior to 1970, some allegedly intact, under a CIA partnership that ended in 1989. AARO says it found no empirical evidence for either. AARO's denial is procedurally notable in its own right: 'The executives, scientists, and chief technology officers of the companies named by interviewees met with the Director of AARO and denied on the record that they have ever recovered, possessed, or engaged in reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology.' AARO does not say which executives, at which companies, on what date, and describes no verification step beyond the meeting itself. Under this board's sourcing rule, that is an artefact of a statement, not evidence of the fact asserted.

What makes the allegation structurally survivable rather than merely unproven is the regulatory architecture around a company like Lockheed Martin. Industrial security oversight of cleared contractors is normally exercised by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency under the National Industrial Security Program. But 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) provides that 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07.' A carve-out programme is therefore a cleared contractor facility from which the government's own standing industrial security inspector has been formally removed by name, at the direction of the second-ranking official in the Department.

The congressional side is narrowed by the same directive. DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued 12 September 2024, states at Section 3.1.g: 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.' That is a standing prior-restraint on contractor-to-Congress disclosure inside the SAP world, in an unclassified, publicly posted directive. The statutory reporting channel is narrower still: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) lets the Secretary of Defense waive the content of any SAP report to the defence committees on a case-by-case national security determination, in which case the information goes 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - eight people, not four committees.

So the record on Lockheed Martin has an unusual shape. Two witnesses under oath, one of them a former Pentagon official, describing the same blocked transfer with the same missing Secretary of the Air Force memorandum. An official report that catalogues the allegation, does not name the company, and reports an unverified denial from unnamed executives. A statutory and regulatory framework that would make exactly this kind of holding invisible to the ordinary inspection and reporting machinery. And, on the other side of the ledger, no contract, no facility designation, no shipping document, no inventory, no subpoena, no inspection, and no on-the-record statement from Lockheed Martin responding to sworn testimony that named it.

dossier.whatItIs: The Central Intelligence Agency is the United States civilian foreign intelligence service. Its documented involvement with the UFO question runs from the Office of Scientific Intelligence study group of 1952 through its convening of the Robertson Panel in January 1953 to its management of the U-2 and OXCART cover stories through the 1950s and 1960s. Its own in-house historian published a detailed account of that record in Studies in Intelligence in 1997.
dossier.whyImplicated: The CIA is the only agency in this dossier set that has published, in its own classified-origin journal, a first-person institutional admission that it directed the government to debunk UFO reports, concealed its sponsorship of the panel that recommended doing so, and knowingly allowed the Air Force to issue misleading and deceptive statements about more than half of all UFO reports for over a decade. That is not an allegation; it is the CIA's own historian describing the machinery of a UFO cover story and calling it by name. Once an agency has demonstrably run one UFO cover story for a real classified programme, the argument that it would not run a second for a different one loses its force. The Agency also sits at the point in the concealment argument where a recovery capability would have to live if the operations occurred on foreign soil, and it has not appeared among the agencies transmitting records to the statutory National Archives collection.
dossier.narrative:
The primary document here is Gerald K. Haines, CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-90, published in Studies in Intelligence in 1997 and posted on the Agency's own website. Haines was a government historian with access to Agency files. What he wrote is more damaging to the Agency's credibility on this subject than anything a critic has written.

The Robertson Panel convened in January 1953 at CIA's instigation, following a recommendation from the Intelligence Advisory Committee to enlist selected scientists to review and appraise the available evidence in light of pertinent scientific theories. The panellists had expertise in nuclear physics, high-energy physics, radar, electronics and geophysics. Their formal conclusion was that there was no evidence of a direct threat to national security and no evidence of extraterrestrial visitation. Their operational recommendation was something else entirely. Haines writes that to meet these problems, the panel recommended that the National Security Council debunk UFO reports and institute a policy of public education to reassure the public of the lack of evidence behind UFOs. It suggested using the mass media, advertising, business clubs, schools, and even the Disney corporation to get the message across. In the same breath, reporting at the height of McCarthyism, it recommended that private UFO groups including the Civilian Flying Saucer Investigators in Los Angeles and the Aerial Phenomena Research Organization be monitored for subversive activities.

That is a US intelligence agency recommending, at national security council level, a domestic public-opinion management campaign on a scientific subject and the surveillance of American civil society organisations that took an interest in it. The Agency then concealed its own role. When public pressure built for release of the panel report in 1956, Philip Strong, Deputy Assistant Director of the Office of Scientific Intelligence, refused to declassify it and declined to disclose CIA sponsorship of the panel. Haines records that the Agency instead prepared a sanitized version which deleted any reference to CIA and avoided mention of any psychological warfare potential in the UFO controversy. When Donald Keyhoe told Mike Wallace on CBS in March 1958 that the CIA was deeply involved and had sponsored the panel, the Agency held firm to its policy of not revealing its role in UFO investigations and refused to declassify the full report.

The U-2 passage is the strongest single piece of documentary evidence anywhere in the official record that the United States Government has deliberately generated false explanations for aerial phenomena and sustained them for years. Haines writes that Air Force BLUE BOOK investigators aware of the secret U-2 flights tried to explain away such sightings by linking them to natural phenomena such as ice crystals and temperature inversions, that by checking with the Agency's U-2 Project Staff in Washington they were able to attribute many UFO sightings to U-2 flights, and that they were careful, however, not to reveal the true cause of the sighting to the public. He then reports that according to later estimates from CIA officials who worked on the U-2 and OXCART projects, over half of all UFO reports from the late 1950s through the 1960s were accounted for by manned reconnaissance flights, namely the U-2, over the United States, and that this led the Air Force to make misleading and deceptive statements to the public in order to allay public fears and to protect an extraordinarily sensitive national security project. Haines adds that while perhaps justified, this deception added fuel to the later conspiracy theories and the coverup controversy of the 1970s.

The Agency also drafted, and then abandoned, a National Security Council Intelligence Directive on UFOs following the Robertson Panel findings. A directive of that class would have assigned standing intelligence community responsibility for the subject. That it was drafted at all establishes that the Agency treated UFOs as a candidate for permanent national intelligence tasking in 1953.

The modern allegations against the Agency are thinner and must be marked as such. Journalist Ross Coulthart has reported, on the basis of David Grusch and other sources, that an office within CIA has coordinated crash retrievals on foreign soil for many years. No document supporting that has been released, no named official has confirmed it on the record, and this board carries it at Tier 3 as a research direction rather than a finding. AARO's Volume I addresses a related allegation and reports that a named former CIA official signed a memo rejecting the claim that he managed the movement of and experimentation on off-world technology, which is an on-the-record denial obtained by an interested party rather than a document from the period.

What can be said cleanly is this. AARO states it partnered with CIA archives for the historical review, so the Agency's UAP holdings were at least nominally opened to the office writing the government's history. Yet as of 22 May 2026 the CIA does not appear among the seven organisations with a transmittal in the National Archives UAP Records Collection. Luis Elizondo, testifying in November 2024, named the CIA first among the agencies that play a role in the UAP issue while no one seems to be in charge, leading in his words to unchecked power and corruption. An agency with a published institutional history of running UFO cover stories, no statutory records transmittal, and a named place in sworn whistleblower testimony belongs on this map.

dossier.whatItIs: Immaculate Constellation is the name of an alleged unacknowledged special access program that entered public reporting in October 2024 through the journalist Michael Shellenberger and entered the Congressional Record on 13 November 2024. According to the whistleblower report Shellenberger delivered to the House Oversight Committee, it was created by the Department of Defense in 2017 after the New York Times published on AATIP, and functions as a central or parent USAP consolidating UAP observations from tasked and untasked collection platforms. The Department of Defense has stated it has no record of any such program.
dossier.whyImplicated: The allegation is not that a secret exists but that a specific legal mechanism was used to keep it from Congress. Shellenberger's sworn written testimony states that a source told him the SAP 'is controlled by the White House and executed and administrated by the DOD to avoid compliance with Title 10 of the United States Code', adding: 'It is essentially a DOD Program, as the White House directed the SECDEF to run it. But that's the loophole.' The same testimony identifies the statutes that should have compelled notification - 10 U.S.C. 119 and 50 U.S.C. 3093 - and asserts that the White House has a loophole for non-covert-action waived programs. That is a falsifiable structural claim about how a compartment can be run without triggering either SAP notification to the congressional defense committees or covert action findings to the intelligence committees. If true, it explains the entire pattern of this board: programmes that no oversight body can locate because no oversight body was ever the notification recipient.
dossier.narrative:
In October 2024 Michael Shellenberger, founder of the outlet Public, reported that a current or former US government official acting as a UAP whistleblower had provided him a report naming an active and highly secretive Department of Defense unacknowledged special access program. On 13 November 2024 he appeared under oath before the House Oversight Committee and the twelve-page document was entered into the Congressional Record from the dais.

His written testimony sets out the constitutional frame before it names anything. It cites 10 U.S.C. 119 and 50 U.S.C. 3093 - the SAP notification statute and the covert action statute - and states: 'DEPSECDEF must notify congress regarding DOD SAPs and the President must notify regarding Covert Action. For UAPs this is apparently not happening because the White House has a loophole for non-covert action waived programs.' The whistleblower's own words, as quoted in the testimony, are that 'the Executive Branch has been managing UAP/NHI issues without Congressional knowledge, oversight, or authorization for some time, quite possibly decades.'

The source characterisation of the programme is that it 'is a "strategic intelligence program" that is part of the US military's family of long-standing, highly-sensitive programs dealing with various aspects of the UAP "problem."' The report itself, as quoted in the testimony, says 'IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION serves as a central or "parent" USAP that consolidates observations' of UAPs 'by both tasked and untasked collection platforms.' It 'includes high-quality Imagery Intelligence (IMINT) and Measurement and Signature Intelligence (MASINT) of UAPs', drawn from 'a blend of directed and incidental collection capabilities positioned in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), the upper atmosphere' and at aviation and maritime altitudes. The most common shapes in the dataset are given as 'spheres/orbs, discs/saucers, ovals/tic-tacs, triangles, boomerang/arrowhead, and irregular/organic.'

The incident material is specific enough to be checkable by anyone with access to the underlying databases. One case: orbs surrounding and forcing an F-22 out of its patrol area, in which 'The F-22 broke trajectory and attempted to evade but was intercepted and boxed in by approximately 3-6 UAPs', with one UAP maintaining 'a rigid spatial relationship with the F-22, maintaining its exact position and orientation parallel with the F-22's cockpit despite multiple evasive rolls and maneuvers.' Another: the crew of a Navy aircraft carrier watching a 'small orange-red sphere' rapidly descend from high altitude to 100-200 yards directly above the flight deck. A third, sourced after publication: a roughly thirteen-minute high-definition full-colour video of a white orb emerging from the ocean approximately twenty miles off the coast of Kuwait, filmed from a helicopter, joined mid-video by a second orb, discovered by the source on SIPR.

The testimony also records a warning about the name itself. 'A source warned that simply printing the name "Immaculate Constellation" could trigger government surveillance of me under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of whoever publishes it. "They won't comment on it, but talking about it will put you in the danger zone," I was told.' From the dais that day Rep. Nancy Mace said the same thing out loud: 'And Representative Luna just told me, if I say, "Immaculate Constellation," I will be on some list. Maybe a FISA warrant. So, come at me bro, I guess.'

The Department's response is a records assertion, and Shellenberger printed it in his own testimony: 'DOD spokesperson Sue Gough said, "The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called 'IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION.'"' That is not a statement that the programme does not exist. It is a statement about what a records search returned, made by a public affairs office that would not hold the read-on to an unacknowledged compartment. Mace's framing on the dais captured the structure exactly: '12 pages about this unacknowledged special access program that your government says does not exist.'

Two further items from the same hearing bear on the plausibility of the mechanism rather than the name. Retired Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, formerly the Navy's chief meteorologist, testified: 'I concluded that the UAP information must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency. That is, a compartmented program that even senior officials, including myself, were not read into.' And Luis Elizondo, asked directly by Mace whether he was read into secret UAP crash retrieval programmes, answered: 'We would have to have a conversation in a closed session, ma'am. I signed documentation 3 years ago that restricts my ability to discuss specifically crash retrievals.'

Under questioning from Rep. Clay Higgins, Shellenberger confirmed he knows the report's author - 'I do' - and declined to characterise the author's institutional position. Asked by Mace what the programme's mission is, he answered that it is an unacknowledged special access program whose 'mission is to document UAPs'. He also stated that when he checked the report against existing public cases he 'did not find it based on existing cases; it was new cases for me', which he offered as evidence against circular reporting.

What the record does not contain is any independent corroboration of the name from a second identified source, any document bearing the programme name, or any executive branch statement beyond the records denial. The name has never appeared in an AARO annual report, in any PURSUE tranche description, or in any published DoD product.
dossier.denialPosture: Department of Defense spokesperson Sue Gough is quoted in Shellenberger's written testimony as saying: 'The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called "IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION."' That is a records assertion rather than a denial of existence, and it is the standard formulation available to an office without read-on to an unacknowledged compartment. Rep. Mace characterised it from the dais as a programme 'that your government says does not exist'. No further departmental statement has been made in the twenty-one months since.
openQuestions: The identity and institutional position of the report's author, which Shellenberger confirmed he knows but declined to disclose.
Whether any congressional committee has formally requested a SAP notification search under 10 U.S.C. 119 against the alleged programme, and what the response was.
Whether the 'non-covert action waived program' loophole described in the testimony is a real category in current SAP practice, and which office administers such programmes.

Whether the specific incidents described - the F-22 boxing event, the CVN flight deck sphere, the Kuwait helicopter video on SIPR - correspond to identifiable case numbers in AARO, UAPTF or service databases.
No document bearing the programme name has ever been published; the only artefact in the public record is the twelve-page report entered by Rep. Mace.
Claims elsewhere that former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick denied the programme could not be verified against a primary source for this dossier and are not asserted here.
